en: The Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra, Scroll One; also known as the Sūtra on the Samādhi in Which All Buddhas of the Ten Directions Stand Before One. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty. Chapter One: Inquiry into Matters. Chapter One: Inquiry into Matters. [The Buddha] was staying in the city of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus. Among them were the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Revata, the venerable Ānanda, and so forth, all of whom were arhats—free from outflows, free from afflictions, having accomplished their task, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own goal, exhausted the fetters of existence, liberated through right wisdom, and whose minds were well-liberated like great elephants. They had all long practiced the holy life under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, adjusted his robes to bare one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him: "World-Honored One, I have a question. May the Tathāgata, out of compassion for me, grant me the opportunity to ask. The Buddha said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, you may ask whatever you wish. I shall explain it for you. Then the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, what is the name of this samādhi? By practicing and cultivating which dharmas can a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain this samādhi? The Buddha said to the venerable Śāriputra: "This samādhi is named 'Pratyutpanna' (Present). A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain this samādhi should practice and cultivate the following dharmas: he should be endowed with pure morality, be free from anger, be patient, diligent, joyful, and without sloth; he should be wise, without arrogance, without hypocrisy, without flattery, without deceit, and without guile; he should not be stingy with wealth, nor stingy with the Dharma; he should be respectful toward teachers and elders, and should always maintain a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings; he should not seek gain, honor, or praise, but should instead seek only the Dharma; he should not be attached to robes, food, bedding, or medicine; he should not be attached to the five desires; he should not be attached to the eight worldly dharmas; he should not be attached to the three realms; he should not be attached to the two vehicles; he should not be attached to the marks of the body; he should not be attached to the marks of speech; he should not be attached to the marks of the mind; he should not be attached to the marks of form, sound, smell, taste, or touch; he should not be attached to the marks of the aggregates, elements, or sense bases; he should not be attached to the marks of birth, old age, sickness, or death; he should not be attached to the marks of the past, future, or present; he should not be attached to the marks of self, person, being, or soul; he should not be attached to the marks of emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; he should not be attached to the marks of conditioned phenomena or unconditioned phenomena; he should not be attached to the marks of saṃsāra or nirvāṇa. Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice and cultivate these dharmas, he will be able to attain this samādhi. [End of Chapter One] *Note: This translation follows the structure and content of the extant Chinese text, providing a literal rendering of the opening sections of the *Pratyutpanna-buddha-saṃmukhāvasthita-samādhi-sūtra*. The bracketed sections indicate narrative transitions and clarifications for fluidity.*
The Buddha was staying at Mahāvaṃkāli in Rājagṛha with a great community of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom had attained arhatship, except for Ānanda alone.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Bhadrapāla, who, together with five hundred bodhisattvas—all of whom observed the five precepts—approached the Buddha at the hour of late afternoon. He bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
Together with five hundred śramaṇas, they went to where the Buddha was; they prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Buddha manifested his majestic spiritual power, and there were no bhikṣus in distant lands who did not come.
Immediately, one hundred thousand bhikṣus followed one another to the place where the Buddha was; they came forward, prostrated themselves before the Buddha, and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha again manifested his majestic spiritual power, and the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with thirty thousand bhikṣuṇīs, followed one another to the place where the Buddha was; they came forward, prostrated themselves before the Buddha, and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha again manifested his majestic spiritual power, and the Bodhisattva Rāhula emerged from the great kingdom of Śrāvastī; the Bodhisattva Kātyāyana emerged from the great kingdom of Campā; the Bodhisattva Naradatta emerged from the great kingdom of Pāṭaliputra; the Bodhisattva Susīma emerged from the great kingdom of Kālapināka; the Bodhisattva Mahāsusārthavāha, together with the lay follower Anāthapiṇḍika, emerged from the great kingdom of Śrāvastī; the Bodhisattva Indradatta emerged from the great kingdom of Kauśāmbī; and the Bodhisattva Varuṇadeva emerged from the great kingdom of Śāketa. Each of these bodhisattvas arrived at the place where the Buddha was accompanied by twenty-eight thousand followers. They came forward, prostrated themselves before the Buddha, and all withdrew to sit on one side.
King Ajātaśatru of Rājagṛha, together with one hundred thousand people, came to where the Buddha was; he went forward, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, and Akaniṣṭha-deva each arrived at the Buddha’s location accompanied by several billions of hundreds of thousands of sons of gods; they went forward, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew to stand to one side.

The Dragon Kings Nanda and Upananda, Śaṅkhapāla, Mucilinda, and Anavatapta, each accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of dragon kings, came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves before the Buddha and withdrew to stand to one side.

The Asura Kings of the four quarters, each accompanied by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Asura subjects, came together to where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves before the Buddha and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, there were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; gods, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and humans and non-humans, in incalculable and immeasurable numbers.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; since I have asked it, it is for a specific reason."
"O God among Gods!
If you will listen to my words, I shall now question the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla:
"Regarding that which you ask for its cause, the Buddha shall explain it for you.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla asked the Buddha,
"In what kind of samādhi should a bodhisattva abide?"

The wisdom they attain is like the great ocean and like Mount Sumeru; they harbor no doubts regarding what they hear, never fail to be leaders among men, and will personally achieve Buddhahood, never returning to the cycle of rebirth nor being born again in places of ignorance.
He foreknows all matters of the past and future; he has never been apart from the Buddha, nor even in his dreams.
He is upright and exceptionally beautiful, with a countenance peerless among the multitude.
From his youth, he was always born into families of noble and great lineage; there were none among his parents, brothers, kinsmen, or acquaintances who did not hold him in reverence and affection.

Of high talent and broad learning, his discussions and compositions were far superior to those of others; he maintained his own discipline and standards, always feeling inward shame if he appeared arrogant, and was constantly filled with compassion and pity.
His wisdom and discernment penetrate all things with clarity; there is none who can equal him.

His majestic spiritual power is peerless, and his diligence is difficult to match. He enters into all sutras and penetrates deeply into them; there is nothing among the sutras that he does not understand.

At ease, they enter dhyāna, enter samādhi, and enter emptiness, signlessness, and non-attachment; being fearless regarding these three matters, they preach the sūtras extensively for others and thereby protect them accordingly.
Wherever they wish to be born, they do so at will without impediment.
By the power of their original merit and the power of their faith, they reach many destinations.

Their physical strength is robust; there is no power of desire or attachment that they do not master, and no power of the faculties that they do not possess. They are clear regarding the power of their direction, clear regarding the power of their mindfulness, clear regarding the power of their vision, clear regarding the power of their faith, and clear regarding the power of their aspiration.

In whatever he is questioned, it is like the great ocean, never reaching exhaustion; like the full moon, it shines everywhere, such that there is none who is not moved by its brilliance; and like the sun first rising, or like a torch illuminating its surroundings, it is free from all obstruction.

The mind is unattached, like space, having no place of rest; it penetrates all things, like a diamond drill; it is as stable as Mount Sumeru, immovable; and it dwells with firm correctness, like a door-sill.
The mind is as supple as a goose feather, devoid of any coarseness;
the body has no longing for pleasure, regarding mountains and rivers like a wild beast.
One should always maintain self-restraint and not engage in worldly affairs with others.

If a śramaṇa or a follower of the Way has many disciples whom he instructs, he protects and watches over them all; even if there are those who treat him with contempt or cause him distress, he never harbors a mind of anger, and no māras whatsoever can move him.
He understands all sutras and enters into all forms of wisdom.
Having studied all Buddha-dharmas, there is no one who can act as his teacher;
regarding his majestic power and noble intent, there is no one who can shake them.
The practice of deep penetration always conforms to non-action and is ever supple; it maintains constant compassion toward the sutras and serves all Buddhas without weariness.
It attains all various merits through its practice, reaching its goal with constancy and maintaining a rectitude of faith that no one can disturb.
Its practice is ever pure and clean, and when facing matters, it is able to resolve them without difficulty.
Pure in wisdom, his insight is fully clear; having attained the conduct he delights in, he exhausts the five hindrances. Through the practice of wisdom, he gradually pursues the realm of Buddhahood.
“He adorns all buddha-fields; within the precepts, he purifies the minds of arhats and pratyekabuddhas; whatever he undertakes is brought to ultimate completion.
His meritorious deeds are always foremost, and so too is his instruction of the people.”
Among the bodhisattvas, there is no weariness in their instruction; that which they must accomplish is boundless; and among all other paths, none can equal them.
They have never been separated from the Buddhas nor failed to see them; they constantly keep the Buddhas in mind, no differently than they do their own parents.
Gradually attaining the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas, they fully master all the sutras.
The vision of one with clear eyes is unimpeded, and all Buddhas stand before them.

It is like a master illusionist who, through his sovereign power, conjures various phenomena; these phenomena are produced without prior calculation or thought, and they neither come from anywhere nor go anywhere.
Just as in a magical transformation, one recollects the past, future, and present as if in a dream; all manifested bodies pervade every Buddha-field.
Just as the sun’s reflection in water is seen everywhere, whatever is recollected is attained like an echo, neither coming nor going.

Birth and death are like the division of shadows; thus, what is conceived and cognized is like space. Within all phenomena there is no conceptualization, and there is none who does not look up to them in reverence.
All things are equal and without distinction; this is fully known within the sutras.
The mind is incalculable; it does not cling to any buddha-fields and has no thoughts directed toward anything;
it emerges from all buddha-fields without further obstruction.
They enter all the gates of *dhāraṇī*, such that hearing one thing among the various sūtras, they know ten thousand; they are able to receive and uphold all the sūtras spoken by the Buddhas.

Serving all the Buddhas, they fully attain the powers of the Buddhas and fully attain the majestic spiritual authority of the Buddhas; they are courageous and encounter no difficulties, walking with the gait of a fierce lion, free from all fear.
In all lands there are none who do not employ his words; those who hear them never forget them at any time; and the discourses of all Buddhas are equal and without distinction.
He thoroughly understands the source and is not intimidated by any sutra; whenever he wishes to expound any scripture, he knows how to do so spontaneously, never wearying as the Buddhas are.
He serves as a teacher to those in the world, with none who do not rely upon him; his conduct is upright and expansive, free from flattery or hypocrisy.
He illuminates all lands with clarity, remaining unattached to the three realms, and his actions are without obstruction.

Among the multitude of beings, he has no partiality; regarding the dharmas of the ultimate limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), he has no longing. Upholding the teaching of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) to lead others into the Buddha-way, he is never terrified and is at no time possessed by fear.
He fully understands all the volumes contained within the various sūtras of the Buddha; among the assemblies where he resides, there are none who do not receive his blessings.

Seeing the Buddha’s supreme great compassion, he rejoices; he has mastered and thoroughly penetrated the sūtras taught by the Buddhas. Within the great assembly, he is fearless, and no one in the great assembly can surpass him; his fame extends to the farthest reaches.

He destroys all doubts and difficulties such that none remain unresolved; he is most honored among the sutras and sits with sovereign mastery upon the lion throne. In accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas, he fully understands the ten thousand kinds of languages of the Buddhas and enters into their myriad billions of sounds.
They cherish and honor the sutras of all Buddhas, constantly keeping them in mind at their side, never departing from the compassion of the Buddhas.

They delight in practicing according to the Buddha’s sutras, always following the Buddhas in their coming and going, and remaining ever by the side of spiritual friends without ever experiencing weariness.
"Without dwelling anywhere among the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, they have fully attained their vows and practices;
they deliver and liberate the myriad beings of the ten directions, and through the treasure of wisdom, they have fully attained the treasury of sūtras."
"His body is like empty space, free from conceptualization; he teaches others to seek the Bodhisattva path so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed.
Practicing the Bodhisattva path, he never departs from the Mahāyāna; having attained the Great Vehicle of the vast and ultimate *saṃnāhasaṃnaddha*, he swiftly attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*)."

All Buddhas praise them; they draw near to the stage of the Ten Powers of a Buddha. All that is conceptualized enters therein; all that is reckoned is fully understood; the transformations of the world are thoroughly known; and the matters of success and failure, as well as those who arise and those who perish, are all fully understood.

Entering the ocean of the sūtras, they open the foremost treasury and give it all away in alms; throughout all lands, their practices and vows never cease, and they manifest supreme transformations according to what the Buddhas delight in practicing.
With a single turn of thought, the Buddhas all stand before him; he no longer forms any further aspirations, nor is there any place for rebirth.
He beholds the incalculable Buddha-fields of the ten directions and hears the sutras preached by those Buddhas;
he sees every single assembly of bhikṣus belonging to each Buddha.

At that time, they do not see by means of the eyes of a rishi, an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha; rather, it is not until they pass away from this world and are reborn in that buddha-field that they see them. Instead, while remaining seated right here, they see all the buddhas, hear all the sutras spoken by those buddhas, and receive them all.
"It is as if I were now before the Buddha’s face, seeing the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; thus, I have never been separated from the Buddha, nor have I ever failed to hear the sutras.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla:
"Excellent, excellent!"

Those who have been questioned by you have been greatly delivered and greatly brought to peace; the people of the world are beyond counting, yet both those above and below heaven have all been brought to security.

If you are now able to question the Buddha in this manner, it is because of the merit produced by practicing the stages of the path (*bhūmi-caryā*) during the time of past Buddhas in previous lives; it is because of having made offerings to various Buddhas; it is because of the joy derived from the sūtras; and it is because of practicing the conduct of the Way and maintaining the prohibitions and precepts.
He maintains the precepts himself, practicing purity without defilement, and subsists solely on alms.
He frequently brings together assemblies of various bodhisattvas and instructs them.
For this reason, through supreme great compassion, they maintain an impartial mind toward all people; whenever anyone wishes to see the Buddha at any time, they shall immediately behold him.

Their vows are of an exceedingly vast and profound practice, constantly mindful of the Buddha’s wisdom; they fully uphold the sutras and precepts, possess the Buddha-seed and the noble mind like a vajra, thoroughly know the thoughts in the minds of the people of the world, and always stand before all Buddhas.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla:
"If one were to calculate his merit, it would be beyond reckoning.
The Buddha said:
"In the Samādhi of All Buddhas Standing Before One in the Present, whoever practices this samādhi shall be able to obtain whatever they ask.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I pray that the Buddha will compassionately explain it."
"What the Buddha now teaches brings great liberation and great peace; I pray that the Buddha will manifest the Great Illumination for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva:
"There is one practice of the Dharma which you should always cultivate and maintain, and always guard; do not follow other teachings again, for it is the foremost among all merits."
"What is the foremost practice of the Dharma?
It is this samādhi called 'All Present Buddhas Standing Before One.
Chapter Two: On Practice. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla:

"If there is a bodhisattva whose present mental focus is directed toward the Buddhas of the ten directions, and if they possess such concentration, they shall attain all the sublime practices of a bodhisattva.
What is this concentration?"
Based on the causal conditions of mindfulness of the Buddha, one directs the mind toward the Buddha with an undistracted intention; thereby gaining wisdom, one does not abandon diligence.
One practices emptiness together with virtuous friends—avoiding sleep and not gathering in crowds—shunning evil associates, drawing near to virtuous friends, and maintaining undistracted diligence.

Content with food, not coveting clothing, and not cherishing one's life; leaving behind kin and departing from one's native village; practicing equanimity and attaining compassion; guarding the conduct of the mind, abandoning the hindrances, and practicing dhyāna.

He does not follow after form, does not grasp at the aggregates, and does not enter into decay. He does not dwell on the four great elements, does not lose his mindfulness, and does not crave their nature; he understands impurity.
He does not abandon the people of the ten directions nor does he cling to them; regarding the people of the ten directions, he considers them as "mine," yet he also considers them as "not mine."
One should not exchange all desires for the precepts; one should practice the conduct of emptiness and seek to recite the sutras.
One must not violate the precepts midway, lose the concentration of mind, doubt the Dharma, dispute with the Buddha, reject the Dharma, or cause disorder within the Sangha of bhikṣus.
One abstains from false speech, assists those who dwell in the Way and its virtue, avoids the worldly talk of the deluded, and takes neither pleasure nor desire in it.
When hearing words of the Way, one possesses the desire to hear them and likewise rejoices.
Born from causes and conditions, these beings do not wish to hear of the six flavors.
They practice the five practices to distance themselves from the ten evils;
they cultivate the ten virtues to understand the nine afflictions.
Practicing the eight kinds of diligence and abandoning the eight kinds of indolence constitutes training in the eight bases of mastery;
it constitutes training in the nine reflections and the mindfulness of the Eightfold Path.

Furthermore, one does not become attached to meditative absorption or learning; one is without arrogance and discards conceit. One listens to the preaching of the Dharma, desires to hear the sutras, and desires to practice the Dharma; one does not calculate according to years, nor does one grasp at the perception of a self.

Detached from the people of the ten directions, they do not wish to receive [rebirth] nor crave life; they understand the aggregates (*skandha*) and do not follow delusions; they do not follow after anything that exists and seek the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

They do not desire birth and death, and they greatly fear birth and death; they reckon the aggregates as thieves and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as snakes, and they reckon the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as empty.
Having long dwelt within the three realms of existence in a state of insecurity, do not forget to attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Do not desire sensual cravings; vow to abandon birth and death.
Do not follow the disputes of others; do not wish to fall into birth and death.
"Always standing before the Buddha, one regards the receiving of this body as being like a dream.

Because one has received and accepted [the teaching], there is no further doubt; the mind is without variation, and all conceptualizations are extinguished—the thoughts regarding past events, future events, and present events alike."
"Constantly mindful of the merits of all Buddhas, one takes refuge in them as one's reliance; with a concentrated mind attaining mastery, one does not follow the characteristics of the Buddha’s body.
Regarding all things as a single reckoning, one does not contend with the world; what one does is non-contentious, having understood that which arises from causes and conditions."

Transcending from the stage of Buddhahood, one attains the state within the Dharma; within that Dharma, one attains the lower [realization]. By means of the intention that realizes emptiness, one regards persons as neither existing nor ceasing.
Self-realizing the unconditioned, the keen eye is purified; all is the awakening to non-duality, with the mind abiding neither in the center nor at the extremes.
All Buddhas enter into a single thought-moment; there is no doubt to be keenly observed, and none who can censure.
Because he has personally attained awakening and understanding, the Buddha’s wisdom does not depend on others.
He regards a good spiritual friend as being no different from the Buddha himself; his mind harbors no other thoughts.
As long as he remains with all bodhisattvas, there is never a time of separation, and even all the Māras cannot shake him.
All people are like reflections in a mirror; seeing all Buddhas is like seeing them by day.
Practicing the Dharma in every way is thus the entry into the pure conduct of a Bodhisattva.
The Buddha said:
“By upholding these dharmas of practice, one attains samādhi; having attained samādhi, all the Buddhas of the present stand before one.
For what reason does one attain the samādhi in which all the Buddhas of the present stand before one?”
Thus it is, Bhadrapāla!

If there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who maintain their precepts in full integrity and dwell alone in a secluded place, they should bring to mind the Buddha Amitābha of the western quarter, who is present now.

According to what you have heard, you should keep in mind that ten thousand million *koṭi* of Buddha-fields away from here lies the land named Sukhāvatī, where [the Buddha] preaches the sutra in the midst of a multitude of bodhisattvas; always keep Amitābha Buddha in your thoughts.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"Suppose, for example, there is a person who, while lying down and dreaming, sees all manner of gold, silver, and rare treasures, as well as parents, brothers, wives, children, relatives, and friends, with whom he enjoys himself; his joy and delight are peerless."
Having awakened, he speaks of it to others, and later tears flow from him as he reflects upon what he saw in the dream. Thus, Bhadrapāla!

If a bodhisattva, whether a śramaṇa or a layperson, hears of the western land of Amitābha Buddha, they should keep that Buddha of that direction in mind and not let their precepts be deficient. With single-minded recollection—whether for one day and night, or for seven days and seven nights—if they continue beyond those seven days, they will see Amitābha Buddha; though not seeing him while awake, they shall see him within their dreams.

It is, for example, like what one sees in a dream: one does not know day, nor does one know night; one does not know the interior, nor does one know the exterior. It is not because one is in darkness that one does not see, nor is it because there is some obstruction that one does not see.
"In this way, Bhadrapāla! A bodhisattva’s mind should form this thought:

'At that time, in all the Buddha-fields where there are names such as Great Mountains or Mount Sumeru, whatever places are dark and obscure shall all be opened up; the eyes shall not be obstructed, nor shall the mind be hindered.'"

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not rely on the divine eye to see through, nor the divine ear to hear through, nor the power of spiritual travel to reach that buddha-field; rather than passing away from this world to be born in that buddha-field before seeing him, they see Amitābha Buddha while sitting right here in this very place. They hear the sutras he preaches and receive them all in their entirety; emerging from samādhi, they are able to fully master them and explain them for others.

"It is as if there were a person who heard that in the country of Śrāvastī there was a courtesan named Sumanā; or another person who heard of the courtesan Āmrapālī; or yet another person who heard of Utpalavarṇā acting as a courtesan."
At that time, each of them thought of her;
though those men had never seen these three women before, their lustful minds were immediately stirred upon hearing of them, and they each went to her location within a dream.

At that time, the three men were all in the kingdom of Rājagṛha and simultaneously thought of her; each, in his dream, went to the dwelling of that courtesan and stayed with her, and upon waking, each recalled it for himself.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"I entrust these three persons to you. If you take this matter and preach the sūtra for others, causing them to understand this wisdom and reach the stage of non-retrogression so that they may attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, they shall thereafter become Buddhas named Suvibuddha."
In this way, Bhadrapāla!
When a bodhisattva hears of Amitābha Buddha in this land, they recollect him repeatedly; by virtue of that recollection, they see Amitābha Buddha.
Having seen the Buddha, he asked him:
"By upholding what Dharma should one be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha?
At that time, Amitābha Buddha spoke to this bodhisattva, saying:
"Those who wish to be born in my land should constantly mind me; they should repeatedly and always maintain this mindfulness without ceasing, and in this way, they shall attain birth in my land."
The Buddha said: “Because this bodhisattva practices this mindfulness of the Buddha, they shall be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
They should constantly be mindful that such a Buddha-body is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks, its radiance shines through all things, and its sublime form is beyond compare.”
When preaching the sutras among the community of bhikṣus, one preaches the sutras without destroying or corrupting form (*rūpa*).
What is meant by not destroying or corrupting form?

It is feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the soul (*ātman*); earth, water, fire, and wind; the world and the heavens—upward as far as Brahmā and Mahābrahmā—one does not destroy or corrupt form.
"By means of mindfulness of the Buddha, one attains the samādhi of emptiness;
this is what is meant by 'mindfulness of the Buddha. The Buddha told Bhadrapāla: "Within this samādhi, who is it that shall bear witness?"
My disciples Mahākāśyapa, the Bodhisattva Indradatta, and the Devaputra Susīma—who currently know this samādhi—as well as those who practice and have attained this samādhi, are its witnesses.
"What is the realization?
Realization is knowing that this samādhi is the concentration on emptiness.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"In the distant past, there was a Buddha named Subhūti.

At that time, there was a man traveling through a vast, desolate wilderness who could find neither food nor drink. Exhausted by hunger and thirst, he lay down and fell asleep; while in his dream, he obtained fragrant, sweet, and delicious food, which he then ate."
Feeling his belly was empty, he thought to himself:
"Is everything that exists merely like a dream? The Buddha said:
"Because that person contemplates emptiness, they immediately attain the joy of the dharma of non-arising, and thus attain the stage of Avaivartika.
Thus it is, Bhadrapāla!"

In whichever direction a bodhisattva hears of a Buddha currently residing, they should constantly keep that direction in mind; desiring to see the Buddha, they should practice mindfulness of the Buddha, neither conceptualizing existence nor maintaining the notion of "mine" or a fixed self.

Just as one perceives emptiness when contemplating the Buddha standing there, like precious jewels resting upon lapis lazuli, so does the bodhisattva perceive the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions in their purity.
It is, for example, like a person who has traveled far away to another district or kingdom, and while there, longs for his native village, his household, his relatives, and his property.
In a dream, that person returns to his native village, sees his household and relatives, and joyfully converses with them.
"Having seen this in a dream, upon waking he tells his friends and acquaintances:
'I returned to my native village and saw my family and relatives.
The Buddha said:

"When a bodhisattva hears the name of a Buddha in whatever direction they are facing, they constantly keep that direction in mind, desiring to see the Buddha; thus the bodhisattva sees all Buddhas, as if holding precious jewels upon lapis lazuli."

For example, when a bhikṣu contemplates the bones of a dead person placed before him, there are times he contemplates them as blue, times he contemplates them as white, times he contemplates them as red, and times he contemplates them as black.
Those bones have no one who brings them; nor do those bones exist, nor do they come from anywhere. They are merely conceptualizations produced by the mind.
In this way, the bodhisattva, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, abides within samādhi; whichever direction he wishes to see a Buddha, as soon as he desires to see, he sees it.
For what reason is this so?
Bhadrapāla! This samādhi is accomplished through the power of the Buddha.
There are three matters for one who stands within samādhi by upholding the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power:

upholding the Buddha’s power of majestic spiritual authority, upholding the Buddha’s power of samādhi, and upholding the power of one's own original merit. By means of these three matters, one is able to see the Buddha.
Bhadrapāla, it is like this:

suppose there is a young person, handsome and beautiful, who has adorned himself; he is like one holding a clean vessel filled with fine sesame oil, or like one holding a fine vessel filled with pure water, or like a newly polished mirror, or like flawless crystal. Desiring to see his own reflection, he looks into it and sees his reflection entirely.
"What do you think, Bhadrapāla?
When a person looks at themselves in sesame oil, water, a mirror, or crystal, does any shadow enter from the outside into those things?"
Bhadra replied: "No, O God among Gods!"
Because the sesame oil, the crystal, and the water-mirror are pure and clean, one sees one's own reflection therein;
yet that reflection neither emerges from within nor enters from without.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Bhadrapāla!"
Thus it is, Bhadrapāla!
When form is pure, that which exists is pure; if one wishes to see the Buddha, one sees him immediately.
Upon seeing him, one asks questions; upon questioning, one receives answers. Hearing the sutra, one rejoices greatly and thinks thus:
"From where has the Buddha come?
To where have I gone?
He thought to himself:
"The Buddha comes from nowhere, and I likewise go nowhere.
He thought to himself:
"The three realms—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of non-perception—are merely the products of the mind."

What I contemplate, I immediately see; the mind creates the Buddha, and the mind sees itself. The mind is the Buddha; the mind is the Tathāgata; the mind is my own body. The mind sees the Buddha; yet the mind does not know the mind, nor does the mind see the mind. When the mind has conceptualization, it is delusion; when the mind is without conceptualization, it is Nirvāṇa.

"In these dharmas there is nothing to be delighted in; they are all produced by thought. Even if one were to suppose that thought is empty, even if there were such a thing as thought, it would ultimately be found to be non-existent. Thus it is, Bhadrapāla!
"When a bodhisattva abides in samādhi, what they perceive is like this.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The mind does not know the mind; Though there is a mind, one does not see the mind."
When the mind gives rise to conceptualization, it is delusion; the absence of conceptualization is nirvāṇa.
These dharmas lack solidity; one should always remain established in mindfulness.
For one who understands by seeing emptiness, there is no conceptualization whatsoever.
Chapter Three: The Four Matters “Bodhisattvas have four dharmas by which they swiftly attain samādhi.

What are these four? First, their faith is such that none can destroy it; second, their diligence is such that none can surpass it; third, the wisdom they enter is such that none can equal it; fourth, they constantly attend upon and serve virtuous teachers.”
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four things by which a bodhisattva quickly attains this samādhi.
What are these four?
First, one must not harbor worldly thoughts for three months, even for as long as it takes to snap one's fingers;
second, one must not lie down to sleep for three months, even for as long as it takes to snap one's fingers;
third, during walking meditation one must not rest nor sit for three months, except for the brief intervals surrounding meals.
Fourth, when preaching the sutras for others, one must not hope for their clothing or food and drink;
these are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva quickly attains this samādhi."

What are the four? First, gathering people and leading them to the Buddha’s presence; second, gathering people and causing them to listen to the sutras; third, being free from jealousy; fourth, teaching others to study the Buddha-way.
These are the four.
“Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva quickly attains this samādhi. What are the four?
First, to fashion images of the Buddha or to create paintings for the sake of this samādhi;”
Second, by means of this samādhi, one provides fine silk for others to transcribe it;
third, one instructs those who are conceited to enter the Buddha-way;
fourth, one constantly protects the Buddha-dharma.
"These are the four.
Then the Buddha spoke in verse, praising them:
"One should always delight in faith in the Buddha-dharma; recite the sutras and contemplate emptiness without ceasing. Be diligent to eliminate sleep and sloth; do not be lax for even three months."

"When sitting to preach the sutra, receive and study it with composure and discernment; you must ensure that its application is vast and far-reaching. If there are those who offer worship or gifts, do not feel joy; remain free from greed and longing so that you may quickly master the sutra."

The Buddha’s complexion is like golden light; his body possesses the thirty-two marks, each mark endowed with the merit of a hundred blessings, as upright and refined as if fashioned from celestial gold.

The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future have all already taken refuge in him; the Buddhas of the present are all the most honored among humanity, and one should constantly mindfully make offerings to them.
One should provide for the Buddha with flowers, incense, powdered incense, and complete offerings of food;
one should maintain a benevolent mind. For this reason, the samādhi will not be far removed.
One should constantly provide drums, music, and performances for the Buddha’s mind, always providing entertainment.
To seek this samādhi, one should create an image of the Buddha, complete with all various features and exquisite in every way, with a countenance like golden light.

Regarding this Samādhi of Seeking: in whatever one gives, one should always joyfully bestow it; in observing the precepts, one should maintain purity and lofty conduct; and by casting off indolence, one will before long swiftly attain this samādhi.

When anger does not arise, and one constantly practices a mind of loving-kindness, constantly practices compassion, and maintains an impartial mind free from hatred, one will attain this samādhi before long.

One should be extremely compassionate toward a virtuous teacher and regard them as a Buddha; anger, hatred, envy, and greed must not arise, and one must not be covetous regarding the teachings given in the sutras.
One should firmly uphold these teachings; all the dharmas of the various sūtras should be entered through them, for this is the path of all Buddhas.
A practitioner who acts in this way will attain samādhi before long.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"Bodhisattvas such as these should always delight in being with virtuous teachers with a mind of loving-kindness; they should regard their teachers as if they were Buddhas and serve them with complete devotion."
Bhadrapāla, when a bodhisattva wishes to transcribe this samādhi sūtra or wishes to study it, they should respect their teacher in this way.

If a bodhisattva harbors anger toward a virtuous teacher, holds onto the faults of a virtuous teacher, or regards a virtuous teacher as not being equal to a Buddha, it will be difficult for them to attain this samādhi.
For example, Bhadrapāla!
Just as a bodhisattva with clear vision sees many stars when looking at the constellations at midnight, so it is, Bhadrapāla!

Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, the bodhisattva abides in samādhi and, looking toward the east, beholds several hundred Buddhas, several thousand Buddhas, several ten-thousand Buddhas, and several hundred million Buddhas;
likewise, throughout the ten directions, they behold all the Buddhas.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"This bodhisattva knows and sees everything with the eye of a Buddha.
It is thus, Bhadrapāla!"

If this bodhisattva wishes to attain the samādhi in which all present Buddhas stand before them, they must fully practice giving and maintain the precepts; likewise, they must be complete in patience, diligence, single-mindedness, wisdom, and the wisdom of liberation, possessing these in their entirety.
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Just as a person with clear vision might look upward at midnight and see innumerable stars, and upon reflecting during the day, see them all clearly;

so too does a Bodhisattva who has attained this samādhi see hundreds of thousands of Buddhas beyond reckoning. Having awakened from that samādhi, he perceives them all through mindfulness and freely expounds the Dharma for his disciples."
The Buddha said:

"Just as my eye is pure and constantly perceives the world, so too does the bodhisattva attain this samādhi and perceive incalculable Buddhas. In perceiving the Buddhas, he does not look at their physical marks, but looks only upon the ten powers."
It is not like those in the world who possess greed; by extinguishing all poisons and becoming pure such that they no longer form conceptualizations, the Bodhisattva attains merit in this way.
Hearing this sutra and following it as if it were nirvana;
hearing this Dharma of emptiness within emptiness, one has no fear.
"I shall preach this sutra in this manner for the sake of the multitude of people, so that they may all attain the path of Buddhahood.
The Buddha said:

"Just as my bhikṣu Ānanda is wise and receives and upholds the sutras upon hearing them, so too does a bodhisattva who has attained this samādhi receive and uphold immeasurable volumes of sutras upon hearing them."
The Buddha said:

"Just as the bodhisattvas in the land of Amitābha Buddha constantly see incalculable Buddhas, so too does a bodhisattva who has attained samādhi constantly see incalculable Buddhas; their faith is always accompanied by a heart of compassion, like a thirsty person desiring to drink."

Always possessing supreme great compassion, renouncing worldly affairs, and constantly delighting in upholding and bestowing the sutras—for these reasons, one becomes pure and will attain samādhi before long.
Chapter Four: Parables. The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:

“Bhadrapāla, as for a bodhisattva who seeks the Samādhi of Compassion, once he has attained this samādhi, if he does not practice with diligent application, it is, for example, like this, Bhadrapāla:”

Suppose there were a person who had filled a ship with precious jewels, intending to cross the great ocean; before reaching his destination, the ship was destroyed midway. The people of Jambudvīpa all felt profound compassion, thinking:
"We have lost all those precious jewels."
"In this way, Bhadrapāla!

When these bodhisattvas have heard this samādhi and yet do not write it down, do not study it, do not recite it, and do not uphold it according to the Dharma within it, all the devas and humans will feel great sorrow and compassion, saying:
'Alas, you have lost such a treasure of sūtras for us!'"
"This is because they have lost this profound samādhi.
The Buddha said,
"This sūtra of samādhi is that which the Buddha has entrusted and that which the Buddha has praised."
Those who hear this profound sūtra on samādhi, yet do not write it down, study it, recite it, maintain it, or uphold it according to the Dharma, will instead become increasingly foolish.
Do you consider yourself superior?
By refusing to accept this sutra, your desire for high talent actually leads you to be unwilling to learn this samādhi.
For example, Bhadrapāla!
A foolish son was given a handful of sandalwood by someone, yet he refused to accept it, instead claiming that the sandalwood given to him was impure.
The merchant said to him: "This is sandalwood; do not say it is impure."
"Furthermore, take it and smell it; do you know its fragrance?
Try looking at it; do you know its purity?
But the foolish man closed his eyes, would not look, and refused to smell it.
The Buddha said:
"Those who hear this samādhi and, being unwilling to accept it, instead abandon and discard it, are people who do not uphold the precepts;
to reject this precious sūtra is to be foolish and devoid of wisdom."

Having personally attained the full realization of dhyāna and considered it sufficient for liberation, he conversely calls the world "existent," failing to enter into emptiness and failing to understand non-existence.
Upon hearing of this samādhi, such a person does not rejoice in it, does not believe in it, and does not enter into it; instead, he speaks with derision:
"Does the Buddha even have profound sūtras?"
"Does he also possess majestic spiritual power?
He replied with a counter-question:
"Is there also any bhikṣu in the world like Ānanda?"
The Buddha said: "Those people who follow one who maintains this samādhi will go about in pairs or groups of three, speaking with one another, saying:
'What kind of talk is this? What is being said here? "
"From where was this statement obtained?
It is merely a fabrication concocted by oneself; this sutra was not spoken by the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:
"It is like a merchant who takes a mani-jewel and shows it to a foolish son of a farmer;
the man asks the merchant, 'Appraise this: how much is it worth? The merchant replies:"
"At midnight, in a dark place, one takes this maṇi jewel and places it within the darkness; the light it illuminates reaches as far as the value of the jewels filling its interior.
The Buddha said: "That person is utterly ignorant of its price, and instead describes this maṇi jewel, saying:"
"Is its price equal to that of one cow?
Would it be possible to trade it for one cow?
Thinking that it could not exceed this, [he said: "If you give this to me, it is well; if you are unwilling, so be it."
"In this way, Bhadrapāla!
If a person hears of this samādhi and does not believe it, they will instead distort the form of this sūtra in such a manner.
The Buddha said:

"If a bodhisattva maintains this samādhi, those who receive it will follow its practice; they will be protected on all four sides and be without fear. Maintaining the prohibitive precepts in their entirety, they will attain lofty brilliance and sagacious wisdom, and will enter deeply into teaching it to others."
“A bodhisattva should uphold this samādhi, distribute it to others, and pass it on from one to another, so that this samādhi may endure for a long time.
The Buddha said:
“Foolish people, who failed to make offerings or cultivate merit before the Buddhas of previous lives, instead become arrogant, frequently engaging in slander and jealousy.”
For the sake of wealth and profit, they seek only fame and desire only to engage in empty talk; they do not find a good teacher and are not clear regarding the sutras.
Having heard of this samādhi, they neither believe in it, nor take pleasure in it, nor enter into it; instead, they slander others, saying:
"This person is shameless and has composed this sutra himself; this sutra was not spoken by the Buddha."
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla: "Now I shall speak to you fully: it is thus, Bhadrapāla!

If a seeker of the bodhisattva path—whether a good man or a good woman—were to take these three thousandfold world-systems filled with precious jewels and offer them as a gift to the Buddhas, even if they possessed such merit, it would not equal hearing this samādhi."
"If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing of this samādhi, believes in and delights in it, their merit will be many times greater.
At that time, the Buddha praised them, saying:
"If one were to fill these three thousandfold world-systems with precious jewels and offer them to the Buddha, using them to seek Buddhahood—"
Furthermore, there are other people—those who uphold this samādhi—who are praised by the Buddha; the merit of those who hear and believe in them is manifold greater.
The Buddha said:

"Those who are deluded and arrogant, who lack faith, and who associate with evil friends, will not believe in or delight in this sutra when they hear it; such people are no different from enemies within my own teachings."
When such people who do not uphold the precepts dwell in self-importance, others hear their words from one another and follow them with faith; this constitutes the destruction of the Buddha-dharma.
Those people will tell one another:
"This sutra was not spoken by the Buddha."
[They] directly slandered it in this way.
The Buddha said:
“There are those who have faith in this samādhi; such people have seen past Buddhas in their previous lives. For this reason, I preach this samādhi for the sake of these believers.”
Such people as these constantly protect the Buddha-dharma; those who hear this sutra and believe and rejoice in it should know this: they are not far from the Buddha.
If one is firm in upholding the precepts and always reveres this sutra with a correct mind, it is for such a person that I speak.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"What I have taught is exactly so; it is for this reason that I speak these words.

Now, those who see me preach this samādhi will, in future lives, upon hearing of this samādhi, never doubt it, mock it, or say they do not believe it—except when they are in the company of evil teachers."

Even if they are with a virtuous teacher, their merit is meager; such persons will further associate with evil teachers, and upon hearing this samādhi, they will not believe it, will not delight in it, and will not enter into it.
"Why is this? Because that person has not studied for long, has encountered few Buddhas, and possesses little faith; it is because his wisdom is slight that he does not believe.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this samādhi, do not mock it nor slander it, but rejoice without harboring doubt, neither saying they believe it one moment and disbelieving it the next, but instead delight in writing it, delighting in studying it, delighting in reciting it, and delighting in upholding it."
The Buddha said:

"I have already known and seen this beforehand: that person has not merely performed meritorious deeds under one Buddha, nor under two, three, or ten; they have heard this samādhi under as many as a hundred Buddhas."

In future ages, those who hear this samādhi, write it down, study it, recite it, uphold its scrolls, or at the very least maintain it for one day and one night, their merit shall be incalculable; they will personally attain the stage of *avaivartika* and obtain whatever they wish for.
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:
“Listen as I tell you a parable.
For example, Bhadrapāla!”

Suppose there is a person who takes a single buddha-field and crushes it entirely into dust; that person then takes one of these particles of dust and crushes it completely into as many particles as there are in a single buddha-field; then they take each and every one of those particles and crush them all into dust until they are exhausted, becoming as numerous as the particles in a single buddha-field.
"Bhadrapāla, what do you think?
Are these particles numerous? Bhadrapāla replied:
“Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:

"I have drawn this analogy for you all: suppose there were a bodhisattva who took every single atom from all these buddha-fields and placed one atom in each buddha-field; if he were to fill that many buddha-fields with precious jewels and offer them all as a gift to the Buddhas, it would not equal the merit of hearing this samādhi."

Furthermore, if there is another bodhisattva who, having heard this samādhi, copies it, studies it, recites and upholds it, and explains it to others for even a brief moment, the merit of that bodhisattva cannot be calculated.
The Buddha said:
"If those who uphold this samādhi—whether by writing it, studying it, reciting it, or explaining it to others—attain such merit, how much more so for those who maintain this samādhi in its entirety?"
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“If one were to fill the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system with precious jewels and offer them as alms,
yet fail to hear a sūtra such as this, the merit and blessings thereof would be meager.”
If there are bodhisattvas who seek all virtues, they should expound and practice this samādhi;
by swiftly reciting and chanting the teachings of this sutra, their merit and blessings will be immeasurable.
Suppose as many worlds as there are atoms in a single Buddha-field were all destroyed and ground into dust;
if one were to give away as many precious jewels as there are such atoms in those Buddha-fields as gifts;
yet another who upholds this World-Honored One’s teaching and explains its meaning in four lines to others—[the latter’s merit would be far greater].
This samādhi is the wisdom of all Buddhas; the merit of hearing it is beyond comparison.

How much more so for one who personally explains it, receives and upholds it, recites and contemplates it even for a moment, and further increases their progress as a practitioner—their merit and blessings will be immeasurable.
Even if all beings were to become Buddhas, possessing the purity of noble wisdom and the foremost clarity of insight,
and were to spend more than a hundred million kalpas expounding the merit of a single verse—
extolling its blessings until the attainment of Nirvana— and were to continue chanting its praises for countless billions of kalpas;
One cannot fully exhaustively fathom the merit of even a single verse concerning this samādhi.
If one were to fill all the lands of every Buddha-field— in the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate points, as well as above and below—
with precious jewels and offer them as a gift to the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods.
If there are those who hear this samādhi, their merit and blessings shall exceed those [previously mentioned];
for one who dwells in composure, recites it, or expounds it, no analogy can sufficiently describe its merit.
Such a person will never again give rise to arrogance, nor shall they ever fall into the evil realms;
having understood the profound Dharma without doubt or entanglement, their virtue from practicing this samādhi is thus.
The scholar serves me with such devotion; his virtue is profound and his diligence is universal and unattached.
Increasing his faith and clarity, he acts as a bodhisattva; he diligently studies the samādhi praised by the Buddhas.
I entrust this to you all; constantly exhort and instruct one another to practice with diligence and without negligence.
Encourage yourselves to cultivate the path with courageous vigor, so that you may attain the Great Way and never regress.
Whoever recites and receives this samādhi has already beheld hundreds of thousands of Buddhas face to face;
even if faced with the greatest terrors at the end of time, they shall hold this samādhi and remain fearless.
This bhikṣu who practices thus, having seen me, will always follow the Buddha and never be far from him;
a bodhisattva who hears and studies this samādhi should, in accordance with its meaning, uphold it and explain it for others.
When a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they are then called one of vast and penetrating wisdom;
having reached dhāraṇī, they are praised by the Buddhas, swiftly attaining the Buddha-way with wisdom like the ocean.
Constantly reciting and expounding this samādhi, one should follow the Buddha-dharma and the teachings of the World-Honored One;
by hearing of his lineage, one attains equal enlightenment, exactly as the Buddha has taught, without any difference.
The Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra, Volume One;
The Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra, Volume Two.
Translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema during the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter Five: On Non-Attachment.
The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:
"How should this samādhi of the bodhisattva be understood?"
For example, when the Buddha now preaches this sutra before you, a bodhisattva should form this thought:
"All Buddhas are standing before me.
He should fully cultivate mindfulness of the Buddhas' physical perfection, desiring to perceive each and every one of them with distinct clarity.
One should contemplate that there is no one capable of seeing the crowns of the Buddhas' heads; thus, one should fully cultivate this perception in order to see the Buddhas.
One should form this thought:
"I, too, shall attain such [a state]; I, too, shall attain such a perception of the body; and I, too, shall attain such upholding of the precepts and samādhi."
One should form this thought:
"Should I attain it through the mind, or should I attain it through the body?
Then, one further forms this thought:
"The Buddha is not attained by means of the mind, nor is he attained by means of the body;
one does not attain the Buddha by means of the mind, nor does one attain the Buddha by means of form. Why is this?"
As for the mind, the Buddha has no mind;
as for form, the Buddha has no form.
One does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of this mind or form.
Why is this? Because the Buddha’s form has been exhausted; the Buddha’s sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have also been fully exhausted.
That which the Buddha calls "exhaustion" is not seen or known by the ignorant, but is clearly understood by the wise.
He then had this thought: "By maintaining what kind of mindfulness shall I attain Buddhahood?
Shall I attain Buddhahood by maintaining the body, or shall I attain Buddhahood by maintaining wisdom?"
Again, he had this thought:
"One does not attain Buddhahood by means of the body, nor does one attain Buddhahood by means of wisdom. Why is this?"
The rope of wisdom cannot find it; searching for a self within oneself, it is utterly unattainable. There is nothing to be attained and nothing to be seen.

All dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; to conceive of them as existing is to be attached, and to deny that they exist is likewise attachment. One does not dwell upon either of these two views, nor does one settle upon a middle ground between them.
It is precisely for this reason that it is neither at the extremes nor in the middle, neither existent nor non-existent. Why?
Because all phenomena are empty.
Such is nirvāṇa: it neither decays nor corrupts, nor is it solid; it is neither here nor there, without conceptualization, and unshakable.
"What is meant by 'being unshakable'?
The wise do not engage in conceptual reckoning;
therefore, they are unshakable. Thus it is, Bhadrapāla!
When a bodhisattva sees the Buddha, they contemplate with the bodhisattva-mind that there is nothing to which they are attached.
Why is it said that "nothing exists"?
The sutras state that within the state of non-existence, not being attached, destroying the root, and severing the root constitutes being without attachment.
"In this way, Bhadrapāla! When a bodhisattva maintains this samādhi, they should perceive the Buddha in this manner, yet they should not be attached to the Buddha. Why is this?
If one has any attachment, it will burn oneself.
It is like a large piece of iron that has been placed in fire and heated until it is glowing red; a wise person should not hold it with their hand. Why is this?
It burns a person's hand.
In this same way, Bhadrapāla!
A bodhisattva should not become attached when seeing a Buddha; one should not become attached to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because attachment burns the body.
Upon seeing the Buddha, one should simply contemplate his merits and seek the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"This bodhisattva, within this samādhi, should not have any attachment; by being without attachment, one will swiftly attain this samādhi."
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Like a newly polished mirror or an oil vessel, A woman adorns herself and gazes at her form;
Within it, she gives rise to thoughts of lustful desire, Her licentious and wanton ways utterly deluded and wild."
If one pursues [the Dharma] without reaching sincerity, the Dharma is wasted in vain; driven by form, one burns one's own body, and from this, the afflictions of women arise.
Because one does not understand that phenomena are impermanent and empty, even a bodhisattva who harbors such conceptions is likewise [afflicted].
"I shall attain Buddhahood and reach the deathless nectar, to deliver all people from the afflictions of grief and distress.
Because some harbor such conceptualizations, they do not understand.
The person sought cannot be found, nor is there birth-and-death or nirvāṇa;
dharmas cannot be grasped, like the moon in water, and when observing the Buddha-way, there is no destination.

The wise Bodhisattva should understand this: realizing that all things in the world are fundamentally non-existent, they remain unattached to any person or object, and shall swiftly attain the Buddha-way in this world.
All Buddhas attain the Way through the understanding of the mind; the mind is pure, luminous, and stainless.
Fresh and clean within the five realms of existence, it does not receive form; he who understands this shall realize the Great Way.
All phenomena are formless and free from outflows; for one who is detached from perception, there is emptiness and the emptiness of non-perception.
By severing sensual desire, the mind is liberated; those who understand this attain samādhi.
Diligently practicing to seek the Buddha-way, Constantly hearing that all dharmas are fundamentally pure,
Without seeking through practice, yet not failing to seek— Then this samādhi will not be difficult to attain.
Observing all things as being like space, the mind of the Way is tranquil and truly supreme;
without conceptualization, without volitional action, and without hearing—this is the thorough understanding of the honored Buddha-way.
Seeing all forms without conceptualizing them, the eye is without attachment and without coming or going;
constantly contemplating all Buddhas as equal to space, one has already transcended all worldly pursuits.
That person’s pure eyes are free from defilement; practicing with diligence, they are ever tranquil.
Having fully received and upheld immeasurable sūtras and dharmas, they contemplate and discern this samādhi.
Practicing this samādhi without attachment, one eliminates all darkness and attains a concentrated mind;
yet the Hero of the World is not seen, nor are the sages and worthies—those of various external heterodox paths are bewildered upon hearing this.
One should aspire to the thought of transcendence; with a pure mind, one attains the vision of the Buddhas.
Having beheld all the Buddhas, one no longer sees them; only then does one understand this honored samādhi.
Neither earth, water, nor fire can obstruct them; even the element of wind and empty space cannot conceal them.
Practicing this diligence, they see the ten directions and sit afar to hear and receive the Dharma they transform others with.
As I expound this sutra here, those who delight in the Dharma shall see the Buddha face-to-face;
practicing with diligence and without attachment, they follow only that which is taught by the World-Honored One.
The practitioner thus remains without conceptual thought, single-mindedly listening to the meaning of the Way and giving the gift of Dharma;
constantly mindful of understanding this samādhi, they universally and correctly receive and recite what the Buddha has taught.
All Buddhas of the past have discoursed on the Dharma, and the World-Honored Ones of the future shall do likewise;
praising, proclaiming, and analyzing its meaning, they all join in extolling the teaching of this samādhi.
I, likewise, am the Honored One among men, the unsurpassed father of sentient beings in this world;
having fully understood and realized this eye of the Way, I therefore explain and manifest the Samādhi of Quiescence.
Whoever lectures upon or receives this samādhi, their body shall always be peaceful and secure and their mind shall not be distracted;
this is the immeasurable virtue of all Buddhas, by which they attain the honored path of Buddhahood without difficulty.
Extensively collecting inconceivable numbers of various sutras, Desiring to realize the transformations of all Buddhas,
Swiftly departing from desires and all defilements— This is the practice of the pure samādhi through diligent application.
If one wishes in this present life to see countless Buddhas, And delights in following the Honored Ones to hear and receive the Dharma,
One should swiftly transcend form and eliminate all attachments, Practicing this pure and tranquil samādhi.
Thus, free from greed and anger, having abandoned delusion and discarded both hatred and attachment,
having cast far away ignorance and eliminated doubt— one thus attains the liberation of the Samādhi of Emptiness.
Chapter Six: The Four Assemblies. In the Pratyutpanna Sūtra, Chapter Six, the Four Assemblies, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha:
“It is difficult to fathom, O God among Gods, that you should speak of this samādhi.”
If there is a bodhisattva who has renounced sensual desire and become a bhikṣu, having heard this samādhi, how should he train?
How should he uphold it?
How should he practice it?
The Buddha said:

"If there is a bodhisattva who has renounced desire and become a bhikṣu, and who intends to study this samādhi, recite this samādhi, or uphold this samādhi, he must maintain the precepts with purity; he must not violate the precepts even by as much as a hair's breadth."
What is the bodhisattva’s unimpaired precept?

It is to fully protect all prohibitive laws and to protect every aspect of the conduct regarding entering and leaving [the monastic life]; one must not violate the precepts even by as much as a hair or a fine thread.

One should always be fearful [of transgression] and remain far removed from flattery and deceit; one should fully protect the prohibitions. To act in this way to protect them constitutes the pure upholding of the precepts.
What is meant by a bodhisattva who is deficient in the precepts?
This bodhisattva seeks form.
What is the seeking of form?
The person thinks to himself:
"By means of these merits, may I be reborn in a future life as a deva or as a Cakravartin king.
The Buddha said, "On this account,
this bodhisattva is deficient in the precepts."

If that person has long maintained these practices and these precepts, and has maintained this self-guarded merit, yet desires to be born in a place where one delights in sensual pleasures, this constitutes a violation of the precepts.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"If these bodhisattvas and bhikṣus wish to study this samādhi, they must maintain the precepts with purity, observing them completely and without flattery or deceit."
One who maintains the precepts shall be praised by the wise and praised by the Arhats.
Within the sūtras, one should practice generosity, exert diligence with firm mindfulness, and be full of faith, encouragement, and joy.
One should always serve one's upādhyāya and should serve one's spiritual teacher (kalyāṇamitra).
One should regard as a Buddha the person from whom one hears this samādhi, as well as the place where this samādhi is heard.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"If a bodhisattva regards their teacher as they would regard the Buddha, they will swiftly attain samādhi.

However, if they do not respect their good teacher, treat their good teacher with contempt, or deceive and mock their good teacher—even if they have long studied this samādhi, long maintained it, and long practiced it—if they do not respect their teacher, they will quickly lose it."
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"If this bodhisattva hears of this samādhi from a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, he should regard them as the Buddha; he should show reverence toward the place where he heard the samādhi."
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"Regarding the places where a bodhisattva hears this samādhi, they should not maintain a deceitful attitude toward them.
A bodhisattva must not harbor a deceitful mind; they should always delight in dwelling in solitary seclusion."
Not begrudging one's own body or life, one should not hope for anything others might seek to give; one should always practice begging for food and not accept invitations.

Free from envy, one maintains self-restraint and dwells according to the Dharma, possessing only what is sufficient for one's needs. One should not be indolent while walking in meditation, nor should one sleep or emerge [from retreat].
Thus it is, Bhadrapāla!
Regarding the teaching in this sutra, those who have abandoned craving and become bhikṣus training in this samādhi should maintain themselves in this manner and observe themselves in this manner.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha:
“It is difficult to encounter, O God among Gods, the Dharma you have taught.
Should there be lazy bodhisattvas in future ages who, having heard of this samādhi, are unwilling to apply themselves with diligence, those people will think to themselves:”
"I shall seek this samādhi from the Buddhas of the future.

Why do you say that our bodies are extremely weak, that we have illnesses and emaciation, and that we fear we cannot seek it? Having heard this sutra, why do you become indolent and fail to apply yourselves with diligence?"
Furthermore, if there are bodhisattvas who are diligent and wish to study this sutra, they should be taught to follow the instructions of the Dharma within this sutra.

For the sake of this sutra, they should not spare their own bodies or lives; they should not hope for anything to be gained from others; they should feel no joy when someone praises them; they should not be excessively greedy for alms bowls or robes; they should have nothing to love or crave, and should always be free from desire.
Hearing this sutra, they shall not be indolent but shall always be diligent; such persons will not think:
"I shall seek it only at the place of a future Buddha.
They will instead think to themselves:
"Even if my sinews, bones, marrow, and flesh were all to wither and rot, I would never grow weary in learning this samādhi.
He thought to himself:
"I shall not die of weariness; having heard this sutra, there is nothing but joy."
At that time, the Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Bhadrapāla!"
"What has been taught is without variation; I rejoice in this, and all Buddhas of the past, future, and present likewise rejoice.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"As I have now taught the Dharma, Receive it all and train therein, dwelling in solitude."
Practicing meritorious deeds and maintaining self-restraint— this samādhi is not difficult to attain.
Constantly begging for food and refusing invitations, completely renouncing all sensual pleasures,
and regarding the Dharma teacher from whom one hears this samādhi as if he were the World-Honored One.
There are those who recite and practice this samādhi; they should always be diligent and never indolent.
They must not begrudge the sutra-dharma, and rather than seeking offerings, they should give the sutras away.
Whoever receives this samādhi is truly a son of the Buddha;
those who study and practice it in this manner will attain samādhi before long.

Always exerting effort without indolence, removing sleepiness so that the mind becomes clear and liberated, one should distance oneself from evil associates; only then should one practice according to this Dharma.
Abandoning heedlessness without rest, always relinquishing social gatherings—
if a bhikṣu seeks this samādhi, he should act in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching in this way.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha:
“If a bhikṣuṇī seeks the bodhisattva path and wishes to study this samādhi and maintain this samādhi, by means of which dharmas should she abide, study, and maintain this samādhi?”
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"A bhikṣuṇī who seeks the Mahāyāna and has attained this samādhi, while training in and maintaining it, should be humble and respectful; she should not be jealous, nor should she give way to anger."
Abandon self-conceit and self-importance; turn away from indolence and practice diligence; cast off sleep and do not lie down to rest.
Completely renounce wealth and profit, and maintain total purity and protection; do not cherish your own body or life.
One should always delight in the sūtras and seek extensive learning; one should abandon lust, anger, and delusion to escape the net of Māra.
One should discard fine garments, ornaments, and jewelry; one must not engage in harsh speech, nor should one covet fine alms-bowls or monastic robes.
One should be praised by others, yet must not engage in flattery.
When studying this samādhi, one should respect the good teacher as if they were a Buddha, uphold the teachings within this sūtra, and maintain this samādhi.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“The bhikṣuṇī who practices reverence, Who is free from envy and jealousy, Who has abandoned anger and removed arrogance,
And who has cast aside self-importance— By practicing these things, she attains samādhi.”
One should exert diligence and abandon sleep; casting aside desires and not craving life, one should maintain a single-minded compassion for this Dharma. Seeking samādhi, one should act in this way.
Do not allow a mind of lustful desire to arise; abandon anger, hatred, and delusion.
Do not fall into the net of Māra; one who seeks samādhi should act in this way.
If one studies this samādhi, One should abandon frivolity and renounce attachment to the body;
Casting aside all doubts, One should be sincere and free from artifice.
Abandoning minor kindness, one should always practice great compassion;
Revering the virtuous teacher without ceasing, one should distance oneself from all evils; Seeking samādhi, one should act in this manner.
Those who practice seeking the Dharma with the desire to attain it, Without craving or attachment for their alms-bowls or robes,
And hear of this samādhi from others, They regard them as equal to the Buddha, no different.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha:
"If there are lay bodhisattvas living at home who, having heard this samādhi, wish to study it and wish to maintain it, how should they stand within the Dharma to study and maintain this samādhi?"
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"When a lay bodhisattva has heard this samādhi and wishes to study and maintain it, they should uphold the five precepts with firm purity and dwell in them;
they must not drink alcohol, nor should they cause others to drink."
One must not engage in sexual intercourse with women; one must not do so oneself, nor should one instruct others to do so.
One must not harbor affection for wife or children, nor think of sons or daughters;
one must not think of property.
One should constantly think:
"I wish to abandon my wife and children to go forth as a śramaṇa.
One should always observe the eightfold precepts of the fast, and during the time of fasting, one should always do so at a Buddhist temple.
One should always be mindful of practicing giving, not thinking, "I shall obtain the blessings for myself," but rather giving for the sake of the myriad people;
one should always maintain great compassion toward virtuous teachers, and upon seeing a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, one must not lightly speak of their faults.
"Having performed these practices, one should study and maintain this samādhi.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If there is a lay bodhisattva who wishes to attain this samādhi,"
One should always study to reach the ultimate end, with a mind free from craving or longing.
When reciting this samādhi, one should contemplate the joy of becoming a śramaṇa;
one must not covet wife or children, but renounce wealth and sensual beauty.
Constantly uphold the five precepts and observe the eightfold fast once a month;
during these periods of fasting at the Buddhist temple, study the samādhis until they are mastered.
Do not speak of others' faults, and do not engage in conduct that is disrespectful or conceited.
With a mind free from worldly ambition, one should practice this samādhi;
Reverently honoring all the teachings of the sutras, one should always delight in the Way;
With a mind devoid of flattery and hypocrisy, one should cast away thoughts of stinginess and envy.
"One who studies this samādhi should always practice reverence,
abandon self-importance and negligence, and serve the community of bhikṣus.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha:
“If there is an upāsikā who seeks mahāyāna-samyaksaṃbodhi and, having heard this samādhi, desires to study and maintain it, what dharmas should she practice to study and maintain this samādhi?”
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"If a laywoman seeks the Mahāyāna *samyaktva-niyāma* and, having heard this samādhi, desires to study and maintain it, she should uphold the five precepts and take refuge in the Three."
What are the three? They are:
taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus.

One must not serve other paths; one must not prostrate to heavenly deities; one must not consult auspicious days; one must not engage in frivolous play; one must not be arrogant or self-indulgent; and one must not harbor a covetous mind.
An upāsikā should always be mindful of practicing generosity, take joy in hearing the sūtras, and exert herself in extensive study.
An upāsikā should always respect her virtuous teachers, keeping her mind ever free from weariness or indolence.
"If there be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who pass by, one shall always provide them with seats and hospitality, including food and drink for guests and hosts.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If there be upāsikās who recite this samādhi,"
One should follow the teachings of the Buddha’s Dharma and fully observe the five precepts.
When maintaining this samādhi, one should revere the Buddha,
as well as the Dharma and the community of bhikṣus, and honor one's virtuous teacher.
One must not serve other paths, nor offer sacrifices to the heavens;
those who practice this samādhi shall see people rise to greet them.
