Abandoning killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, they are sincere and refrain from double-tongued speech.
Do not go to taverns; you should practice this samādhi.
Your mind must harbor no greed; you should always be mindful of giving.
Cast away thoughts of flattery and do not speak of others' faults.
"One should always serve with reverence the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, hearing and fully accepting all their teachings of the Dharma; one should train in samādhi in this manner.
Chapter Seven: Bestowing Prophecy In the *Pratyutpanna Sūtra*, Chapter Seven: Bestowing Prophecy, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla asks the Buddha:
"Rare indeed are those who can equal you, O God among Gods!
It is the Tathāgata who has preached this samādhi, which all bodhisattvas delight in practicing with vigor, remaining free from indolence regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, will this samādhi remain within Jambudvīpa?
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva:
"After my parinirvāṇa, this samādhi shall remain manifest for forty years; after that, it will no longer appear."
In the future, during an age of chaos when the Buddhist scriptures are on the verge of being severed, the bhikṣus will no longer accept or employ the Buddha’s teachings.
Subsequently, during that period of disorder, when nations wage war against one another, this samādhi shall once again appear within Jambudvīpa.
"By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, this Samādhi Sūtra shall emerge once again.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla and the Bodhisattva Ratnākara rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, and with palms joined before the Buddha, addressed him:

"In the chaotic age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall together protect this samādhi and uphold this samādhi; we shall fully explain it for others, never growing weary of hearing this sūtra volume."
The Bodhisattvas Mahāsusthita, Kautūhalin, Naradatta, Susīma, Indradatta, and Varuṇadeva addressed the Buddha together, saying:

“After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, during the period of the chaotic age that follows, we ourselves shall collectively protect and uphold this sutra scroll, so that the Buddha-way may endure for a long time.”
"Should there be those who have not yet heard it, we shall together explain it for them and instruct them in this profound sutra;
though few in the world will believe it, we shall all receive it."
Then five hundred people—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—rose from their seats, joined their palms before the Buddha, and stood there, addressing the Buddha:

"In the chaotic age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall hear of this samādhi and each vow to uphold and protect it ourselves. We, these five hundred people, entrust these eight bodhisattvas with this task."

At that time, the Buddha smiled, and from his mouth issued a golden light that reached and illuminated immeasurable buddha-fields throughout the ten directions; it then returned, circled the body three times, and entered through the crown of his head.
Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his *kāṣāya*, and went before the Buddha to pay him homage. Stepping back to stand with palms joined, he praised him in verse:
“His mind is pure and his conduct is undefiled; His supernormal powers are infinite and his great transformations vast.
Having transcended all obstructions and surpassed all wisdoms, His radiance dispels darkness and removes the dust of defilement.”
With immeasurable wisdom and a mind universally liberated, the Buddha, the God among Gods, possesses the voice of a pheasant;
no outsider can move him—by what cause do you smile and emit this wondrous light?

I pray that the Perfectly Awakened One will explain this for me; O Honored One who has compassion for all sentient beings, if there are those who hear the Buddha’s gentle voice, they shall understand and penetrate the Sage’s teachings on transforming worldly conduct.
What the World-Honored One perceives is not in vain; the Teacher of the Sages does not smile without cause.
Who now shall be among those destined for liberation?
O Hero of the World, we pray that you explain this meaning.
Who today dwells firm in the Way and its Virtue?
Who shall attain and give rise to wondrous practice?
Who now receives the profound treasury of Dharma—the unsurpassed Way and Virtue to which all turn?
Who today shall take pity upon the world?
Who shall receive and uphold this teaching of the Dharma?
Who shall firmly establish others in the wisdom of the Buddha?
“World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain this for us.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses to Ānanda:
“The Buddha says to Ānanda!”
"Do you see them?
These five hundred people stand before you; their hearts are filled with joy as they sing this hymn of praise:
'We, too, shall attain this Dharma.'"
With serene and joyful countenances, they gazed reverently upon the Buddha and asked,
"When shall we ourselves attain such as this?
All stood with bated breath, praising the Buddha.
"We shall surely attain such [a state] as this.
These five hundred people now present, though their names differ, are identical in their fundamental practice;
they always delight in receiving and upholding this profound sutra, and so shall it be in future ages as well."
Now I entrust this to you all: the Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and knows their origin.
These beings have not seen only a single Buddha, nor did they attain this wisdom by relying on this alone.

He clearly illumined that person’s past lives; having previously encountered eighty thousand Buddhas, five hundred people remained on the Path, constantly understanding the meaning of the sutras and striving to bring their practice to fulfillment.
Exhorting and assisting countless bodhisattvas, They constantly practice compassion and protect the sutras and the Dharma;
Exhorting and transforming all the people, Causing them all to attain the practice of the Great Way.
Knowing and seeing the World-Honored Ones of past ages, beholding eighty billion nayutas in number,
their names and virtues universally great, they liberate the mind and protect this Dharma through its three turnings.
In this present life, they receive my teaching; they distribute and make offerings to these relics.
With serene composure, they accept and practice what the Buddha has transformed [into Dharma], reciting it all and receiving that which has been entrusted to them.
Having deposited [the scriptures] in stūpas, temples, and within mountains, or entrusted them to devas, nāgas, and gandharvas,
and having each transmitted the scrolls in turn, they shall, at the end of their lives, be reborn in the heavens.
When their lifespans in the heavens have ended, they return to the world, each being born into different lineages;
they shall again undertake this practice of the Buddha-way and distinguish this sutra according to their vows.
Because they love and delight in this sutra-dharma, they seek it and immediately obtain it to uphold and practice;
they cause countless people to hear it, their joy being immeasurable and their minds peerless.
These wise ones do not weary of the Dharma; they do not crave their bodies or their lives.
Having subdued all non-Buddhist outsiders, they bestow the scriptural teachings to fulfill their aspirations.
No one shall be able to attain this sutra-dharma, nor those who uphold, recite, or expound it;
yet these fourfold assemblies now standing before me, this multitude of five hundred, are capable of upholding it.
These eight bodhisattvas— Bhadrapāla, Ratnākara, Naradatta, Mahāsusārthavāha, Varuṇadeva,
Indradatta, Susīma, and Guhagupta— together with bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and upāsakas,
reverently upheld this profound and wondrous Dharma of the supreme meaningful phrases.
Constantly using the Way of the Sūtras to take pity on the world, they proclaim and spread the Vaipulya teachings everywhere.
The eight bodhisattvas, Bhadrapāla and the others, are heroes among the assembly of five hundred;
they shall always uphold the Vaipulya sūtras and remain unattached to worldly customs.
Releasing all bonds through the wisdom of emptiness, with the purple-gold hue and the marks of a hundred merits,
you constantly practice compassion to deliver sentient beings, bestowing peace and extinguishing all defilements.
After their lives have ended, they shall be born into the family of the Dharma, never again returning to the three evil realms;
following one another through successive generations, they shall always remain in harmony, and thereafter attain the supreme path of the Buddha.
Having already cast off the eight states of woe, and being far removed from all evil realms,
his meritorious conduct is beyond praise, and the blessings he receives are immeasurable.
When we again encounter Maitreya Buddha, may we all with one mind go to take refuge;
together we shall make offerings with equal compassion and reach the state of unsurpassed quiescence.
Their minds are entirely harmonious and unified; with upright intent, they serve the Honored One among Men.
Without relying on worldly affairs, they attain the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) and swiftly reach the practice of the unsurpassed Great Way.
He shall constantly uphold this sūtra-dharma, reciting it with diligence from dawn until dusk;
planting manifold roots of merit and cultivating pure conduct, his realization of the truth will be such as this when he beholds Maitreya.
Thus, the Buddhas arisen in this Bhadrakalpa, out of compassion for the world, radiate light;
wherever they may be, they universally uphold the Dharma and serve the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Having made offerings to all the Heroes of the World, and seeing that the Honored Ones of the three times are free from all poisons,
one shall swiftly attain the supreme path of the Buddha— inconceivable and immeasurable.

Among them, there were those who first attained the Way of the Buddha, and later generations successively made offerings to one another for incalculable kalpas and nayutas; it was only at the very end that this practice finally ceased.
Thereupon the lay devotees Bhadrapāla, Ratnākara, Naradatta, Susīma, and Guhagupta—
each of whom had previously seen Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— [arose].
One should always serve and follow the transformation of the True Dharma, proclaiming the immeasurable teachings of all Buddhas;
such practice of the Way is infinite and beyond praise, continuing through countless billions of kalpas.
If there should be anyone who upholds this name, wherever they may travel— even in their dreams—
such a courageous leader of the world shall all attain the unsurpassed path.

If there are those who behold [the Buddha] or hear his voice, and their hearts are filled with joy and exultation, they shall all attain the Way of the Buddha without further doubt; how much more so for those who respectfully receive and make offerings?

If one should harbor anger, utter insults, or strike with a malicious intent, even such a person may yet attain Buddhahood through the majestic power and grace of these eight; how much more so for those who show them reverence?
The Dharma he has received is inconceivable; his fame and lifespan are immeasurable.
His radiance is boundless and his virtues are beyond doubt; his wisdom is infinite, and so too are his practices.
Constantly obtaining face-to-face audiences with immeasurable Buddhas, their pure precepts as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
they thereupon practice giving extensively and universally, thereby seeking the unsurpassed Way.
Even if one were to speak of its blessings for countless billions of kalpas, No one could reach the limit of its merit.
For those who receive this sutra-dharma and recite and practice it, Reaching the Great Way will no longer be difficult.

Those who love and delight in this sutra scroll, who receive, recite, chant, uphold, and expound it—know that they are among the five hundred people; their hearts love and delight in it, never doubting.
If one gives this sutra-dharma as a gift, delights in the meaning of the Way, increases diligence, practices pure precepts,
and eliminates sleep and sloth, then attaining this samādhi will ultimately not be difficult.
Desiring to attain peace and security, one should spread the sutras and precepts;
A bhikṣu who studies while dwelling in seclusion, Constantly practicing alms-gathering and knowing contentment, Will find that this samādhi is ultimately not difficult to attain.
Abandoning all clamor, do not accept invitations; let the mouth not crave flavors and cast off sensual desire.
One who hears this Dharma from another should honor them as the World-Honored One and constantly serve them.

Having cast aside stinginess and greed to receive this Dharma, severing lustful desire and abandoning folly, one should give rise to the mind of the Great Way without doubt; only then should one study and practice this samādhi.
Practicing without attachment and relinquishing all desires, one should always remain self-restrained, casting off anger and resentment.
Diligently practice the teachings of the Buddha-dharma, And only then receive and study this samādhi;
Do not covet men, women, or possessions, Remain far removed from arrogance, concubines, and wives;
Practice the Way while living at home with constant shame and remorse, And only then learn to recite this samādhi.
Acting with gentleness and free from a mind of malice, Not delighting in slander and abandoning all evils,
Not seeking the attainment of the Dharma-patience through physical form, One should skillfully recite this samādhi.
If a bhikṣuṇī studies this Dharma, she should always be respectful and abandon arrogance;
by distancing herself from frivolity and conceit, she will find this samādhi not difficult to attain.
Constantly practicing diligence and eliminating sleep and sloth, she does not reckon in terms of "self" or "others," nor of persons or things.
Those who delight in the Dharma do not begrudge their lives; only then do they study and recite this samādhi.

They restrain lustful thoughts and abandon attachments; with no heart of anger and casting aside flattery, they shall never again fall into the net of Māra—by upholding this samādhi, one attains such results.
Treat all sentient beings with equanimity, And remove the dust of heedlessness.
Being free by nature from violence and coarse speech, Only then should one study and recite this samādhi.
Regarding the alms bowl, robes, and clothing, One must not harbor even a moment’s craving or attachment.
Venerating the virtuous teacher as if they were a Buddha, one should then study and recite this samādhi.

By attaining wholesome benefits and leaving the evil realms behind, and with a single mind believing and delighting in the teachings of the Buddha-Dharma, one will distance oneself from all eight difficult conditions; those who uphold this sūtra shall obtain such results.

Chapter Eight: On Protection. In the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, Chapter Eight on Protection, the bodhisattvas Bhadrapāla, Ratnākara, Guhagupta, Naradatta, Susīma, Mahāsusārthavāha, Indradatta, and Varuṇadeva, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced. These eight bodhisattvas took five hundred garments of fine *karpāsa* silk, offered precious jewels as gifts, and dedicated their own bodies to serve and make offerings to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“These Bhadrapāla and his peers are teachers among five hundred bodhisattvas who constantly uphold the Middle Way of the True Dharma. Those who assemble to follow their teachings are all filled with joy—joyful minds, timely minds, pure minds, and minds that have cast away desire.”
At that time, the five hundred people all stood before the Buddha with their palms joined. The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By maintaining how many things does a bodhisattva attain this samādhi?”
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"There are four matters by which a bodhisattva quickly attains this samādhi."
What are the four? First, not believing in other paths; second, severing craving and desire; third, practicing according to the Dharma; and fourth, being free from the arising of greed.
"These are the four [conditions] by which a bodhisattva quickly attains this samādhi.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"If there is a bodhisattva who studies this samādhi—whether by upholding it, reciting it, or guarding it—they will immediately attain five hundred merits in this very life."
For example, Bhadrapāla!

A bhikṣu with a mind of loving-kindness will never be harmed by poison, never be struck by weapons, cannot be burned by fire, will not die when entering water, and no sovereign can find an opportunity to harm him.

In this way, a bodhisattva who maintains this samādhi will never be harmed by poison, never be struck by weapons, never be burned by fire, never be drowned by water, and never be taken advantage of by kings or emperors.
For example, Bhadrapāla!

When the kalpa is exhausted and destroyed by fire, even if a bodhisattva who maintains this samādhi should fall into that fire, the fire will immediately be extinguished, just as a large jar of water extinguishes a small fire.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"What I have said is without exception.

For a bodhisattva who upholds this samādhi, whether it be a sovereign, a thief, water, fire, a nāga, a snake, a yakṣa spirit, a fierce beast, a great python, a crocodile, a lion, a tiger, a wolf, a dog, a human, a non-human, a monkey, a preta, or a kumbhāṇḍa spirit—if they wish to harass the person, or wish to kill them, or wish to seize their bowl and robes, or wish to destroy their meditative concentration and steal their mindfulness—should they intend to strike this bodhisattva, they will ultimately be unable to do so."
The Buddha said, "What I have spoken is without deviation; except for that which was invited by one's own past karma, there is nothing else that can affect it.
The Buddha said:
"What I have spoken is without error.

If there is a bodhisattva who upholds this samādhi, they shall never suffer from eye disease, nor from diseases of the ear, nose, or mouth; their body shall be free of illness, and their mind shall never be sorrowful or distressed."
If this bodhisattva should die or be near death, even if such afflictions should occur, the word of the Buddha would not be otherwise—
except for that which was produced by their past karma. "Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

All the devas praise this bodhisattva; all the nāgas praise him; all the yakṣas and spirits praise him; all the asuras praise him; the garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans all praise this bodhisattva; and all the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, praise this bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla! This bodhisattva is protected by the devas;

he is protected by the nāgas. The Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, and Brahmā Sahāmpati all protect this bodhisattva. Yakṣa spirits, gandharva spirits, asura spirits, garuḍa spirits, kiṃnara spirits, mahoraga spirits, and whether they be humans or non-humans, they all together protect this bodhisattva. All the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, also together protect this bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla! This bodhisattva is revered and loved by the devas;

likewise, the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, mahoragas, and whether they be humans or non-humans, all together revere and love this bodhisattva. Even the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods—who are entirely free from desire—because of their virtue and the Way, also revere and love this bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla! All the devas wish to see this bodhisattva;

all the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas—whether humans or non-humans—all long and delight in seeing this bodhisattva. Each of the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, wishes for this bodhisattva to go to their respective abodes—for the sake of the people, they wish him to go."
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

All the devas come to where this bodhisattva dwells; likewise, all the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and whether humans or non-humans, all come to where this bodhisattva dwells to meet with him."

The Buddhas, the Gods among Gods—bodhisattvas see them not only during the day, but even at night within their dreams; they may see the bodies of the Buddhas, or each Buddha may individually proclaim his own name.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

Regarding those sūtras that this bodhisattva has not yet recited and those scriptural volumes he has not previously heard, by the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi, he will obtain the names of all those sūtra volumes within his dreams; he will see each one and hear the sound of each sūtra. If he does not obtain them during the day, he will see and obtain them all within his dreams at night."
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"Whether for one kalpa or even more than one kalpa, were I to speak of the merits of this bodhisattva who upholds this samādhi, I could not reach their end; how much less so for one who strives diligently to attain this samādhi?"
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“If there is a bodhisattva who studies and recites this, The samādhi of the tranquil and fixed meaning taught by the Buddha,
Even if one were to wish to praise its merit, It would be like removing a single grain of sand from the banks of the Ganges.”
Swords, blades, spears, and halberds shall not wound them; thieves, bandits, and enemies shall be unable to harm them;
kings and ministers shall approach them with joy—by studying this samādhi, one attains such results as these.
The venomous viper harbors poison and is truly fearsome; yet upon seeing that practitioner, its poison is swiftly dispelled.
It no longer gives way to anger or emits foul breath—by reciting this samādhi, one attains such results.

Neither enemies nor grudges can prevail against them; when devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and kinnaras behold their majestic radiance, they all fall silent. By studying this samādhi, one attains such as this.
In the mountains and wilds, the predatory wolves and great pythons, lions, fierce tigers, deer, and monkeys harbor no intent to harm;
they conceal their venom and all come to personally protect this practitioner.
Even malevolent spirits who seize the souls of men, as well as devas and human beings harboring harmful intentions, [are likewise pacified].
Touched by his majestic spiritual power, they submit naturally; By studying this samādhi, one attains such as this.
That person is free from illness and suffering, With keen faculties of hearing and sight, unobstructed.
Their speech is eloquent and wise, most distinguished and eminent; One who practices this samādhi will swiftly attain this.
Such a person shall never fall into hell, nor enter the realms of hungry ghosts or animals;
in every life they are born, they will know their past lives—by studying this samādhi, one attains such as this.
Ghosts and spirits, and gandharvas, protect them together; so too do the devas and human beings, as well as the asuras and mahoragas—those who practice this samādhi obtain such [protection].

All the devas together extol his virtues; gods, humans, nāgas, ghosts, and kinnaras—all Buddhas praise him so that he may have his wishes fulfilled, as he recites and expounds the sūtras for the sake of others.
Such a person’s resolve for the Way is non-retrogressive; the meaning of their Dharma-wisdom is inexhaustible.
Their countenance is beautiful and radiant beyond compare, as they recite and study this sutra to transform and enlighten others.
When nations strike one another down and the people fall into chaos and disorder, and when famines repeatedly arrive bringing bitter destitution—
those who can recite this sutra and transform others shall never lose their lives prematurely amidst such conditions.
Valiantly subduing all demonic activities, their minds are fearless and their hair does not stand on end;
their meritorious conduct is inconceivable—by practicing this samādhi, one attains such as this.
Through the transformations of malevolent spirits and sorcery, or through foul and turbid heterodox practices,
none shall ever be able to harm their person, for they delight in the Dharma and have realized the fundamental source.
All together shall sing his virtues— this son of the Buddha, who is fully endowed with the wisdom of emptiness—
and in the future, during the final age, he shall obtain this sutra with his own hands.
Always practicing with diligence and harboring joyful exultation, with one mind in harmony and gladness, they honor this Dharma;
receiving, upholding, expounding, reciting, and chanting the sutra scrolls—now I speak of this for their sake.
Chapter Nine: The Buddha Kṣemadharman in the Pratyutpanna Sūtra. Chapter Nine: The Buddha Kṣemadharman. The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:

"In the distant past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Kṣemadharman, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He was most honored in the world, bringing stability to the world;
he was a great light within the sūtras, and throughout heaven and earth he was titled 'God among Gods'."

At that time, there was a son of a householder named Sudatta, who arrived at the dwelling of the Buddha Kṣāranadya together with twenty thousand people; having paid homage to the Buddha, he withdrew to sit to one side.
The elder’s son Sudatta asked the Buddha Kṣemadharśin about this samādhi.
Knowing what was in the mind of the elder’s son Sudatta, the Buddha Kṣemadharśin then expounded this samādhi for him.
Having heard this samādhi, the elder’s son Sudatta was filled with great joy; he immediately memorized it in its entirety, became a śramaṇa, and sought this samādhi for eighty thousand years.
At that time, the elder’s son Sudatta heard many sūtras from the Buddha—sūtras he had previously heard from countless Buddhas—and his wisdom became exceedingly lofty and brilliant.
After his life had ended, the elder’s son Sudatta was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; subsequently, he descended again from heaven to be born in the world.
At that time, within that same kalpa, there was another Buddha named Śvetaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, the Buddha was born into a Kṣatriya family. Then, the elder’s son Sudatta again heard of this samādhi from the Buddha and sought it once more.
Subsequently, during that same kalpa, there was another Buddha named Rāvaṇa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who was of Brahmin descent. The elder’s son Sudatta again [heard of it] from him.
At that time, the elder’s son Sudatta again received this samādhi from the Buddha and sought to maintain it for eighty-four thousand years.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"The elder’s son Sudatta shall, after eighty-four thousand kalpas, attain buddhahood; his name shall be Dīpaṃkara."
At that time, the elder’s son Sudatta was eminent and courageous among men, and his wisdom was exceedingly vast.
The Buddha said,
"Do you see this samādhi?"
Bhadra! Your benefit is such that it causes people to achieve the Way of the Buddha.
If there are bodhisattvas who attain this samādhi, they should study and recite it, uphold it, teach it to others, and preserve it; those who do so will attain Buddhahood before long.
Do you understand, Bhadrapāla?
This samādhi is the eye of bodhisattvas, the mother of all bodhisattvas, that which all bodhisattvas rely upon and look up to, and that from which all bodhisattvas are born.
"Do you know it, Bhadrapāla?
This samādhi destroys darkness and brings illumination to all that is above and below heaven."
"Do you understand, Bhadrapāla?

This samādhi of the bodhisattvas is the treasury of all Buddhas, the ground of all Buddhas; it is the spring from which the ocean of precious jewels wells forth, and the source of immeasurable merit and benefit."
The scriptures of the wise and enlightened should be understood in this way:
such is that which emerges from samādhi; from within it emerge the Buddhas, the hearing of the sūtras, and the correct establishment in the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four foundations of mindfulness?
First, one contemplates one's own body, contemplates the bodies of others, and in contemplating one's own body and the bodies of others, realizes that fundamentally there is no body.

Second, one contemplates one's own sensations, contemplates the sensations of others, and in contemplating one's own sensations and the sensations of others, realizes that fundamentally there are no sensations.
Third, one contemplates one's own mind and contemplates the minds of others; yet, in contemplating one's own mind and the minds of others, there is fundamentally no mind.
Fourth, one contemplates one's own phenomena and contemplates the phenomena of others; yet, in contemplating one's own phenomena and the phenomena of others, there are fundamentally no phenomena.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"Who would believe in this samādhi?
Only the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, those who are irreversible (avaivartika), and the Arhats would believe in it."
Those with deluded and confused minds are far removed from this samādhi of standing before the present Buddha.
Why is this? This Dharma requires that one mindfully recollect the Buddha and see the Buddha.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"This bodhisattva should recollect the Buddha, should see the Buddha, and should hear the sutras, yet should not have any attachment. Why is this?
The Buddha is fundamentally without this, and the Dharma has no cause.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally empty and non-existent; each and every one practices the mindfulness of dharmas.

Within these dharmas there is nothing to be grasped; these dharmas are without attachment, as utterly pure as space and the like; regarding these dharmas, what people conceive of is entirely non-existent.
This dharma is non-existent; that which serves as its provisional cause is merely empty and quiescent, like nirvāṇa.
This dharma is non-existent; fundamentally this dharma has never existed, coming from nowhere and going nowhere.
"Human beings originally do not possess this dharma; those who do not cling to it are near, while those who cling to it are far.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"If there are those who maintain this samādhi, they will, by means of mental conception, enter into non-conception to see the Buddha and recollect the Buddha."
Maintaining mindfulness while hearing the sutras and recollecting the Dharma, one who maintains mindfulness must not think of a self and must not become attached to the Dharma.
Why is this? Because there is the maintenance of mindfulness, Bhadrapāla!
If one maintains vigilance yet does not see the Buddha, or if one has attachments as slight as a hair or a speck of dust, one will not attain the Dharma.

To give to others with expectation is not true giving; to observe the precepts with expectation is impurity; to crave the Dharma is to fail to attain Nirvana; and to be flatterers within the sutras is to fail to achieve high wisdom.
Delighting in assemblies and finding joy in other paths, one will ultimately be unable to attain even a single practice.
To dwell on the difficulties within desire, to harbor anger and fail to practice patience, and to feel hatred such that one cannot speak well of others—these are the obstacles.

One who rightly seeks the path of arhatship does not perceive [the self] therein; within the samādhi in which all present Buddhas stand before one, one does not grasp at dharmas that have no place from which they arise, yet one takes pleasure in abiding therein, and because there is attachment, one does not attain emptiness.

A bodhisattva shall never be stingy or greedy; if one is indolent, one will not attain the Way; if one is lustful, one will not enter contemplation; and if one harbors discursive thoughts, one will not enter samādhi.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“These merits are beyond calculation; They uphold the precepts perfectly, free from blemish.
Their minds are pure, detached from defilement and dust; By practicing this samādhi, they attain such as this.”
Should there be one who upholds this samādhi, their wisdom will be universally vast and without deficiency;
they will extensively comprehend all meanings and never forget them, and their meritorious conduct will be as bright as the moon.
If there be one who upholds this samādhi, they will understand and awaken to the inconceivable nature of the mind;
they will clearly know the immeasurable dharmas of the Way, and countless devas shall protect their virtue.
Should there be one who upholds this samādhi, they will always personally behold countless Buddhas face-to-face;
hearing the immeasurable Buddhas preach the Dharma, they are able to receive, uphold, and mindfully practice it everywhere.
If there be one who maintains this samādhi, all evil offenses and diligent sufferings shall be extinguished;
the Buddhas, practicing compassion throughout the world, will all together praise this bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva wishes to behold the countless Buddhas and World-Honored Ones of the future,
they should dwell with single-minded joy in the True Dharma and study the recitation of this samādhi.
Whoever upholds this samādhi possesses merit and blessings beyond measure;
having attained a human body, they are foremost among all, leaving the household life to transcend others through the practice of alms-gathering.
If there are those who obtain this sutra at the very end [of the age], they shall attain the foremost benefit of merit;
the blessings they receive shall be beyond limit, as they abide in this samādhi and achieve such results.
The Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra, Middle Volume;
The Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra, Lower Volume.
Translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema during the Later Han Dynasty.
10. Chapter on Inviting the Buddha. Chapter Ten: Inviting the Buddha.
Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for a meal at my home tomorrow; I pray that the Buddha will compassionately accept this invitation."
The Buddha and the community of bhikṣus accepted the invitation in silence.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla rose and went to the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, saying to her:
"I pray that you will accept my invitation; tomorrow, please join with the bhikṣuṇīs for a modest meal at my home."
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī accepted the invitation. Then,
the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla said to the bodhisattva Ratnākara, "Brother!"
"Let all those from the various commanderies and kingdoms who have newly arrived be invited to assemble at the Buddha's dwelling.
Then, the Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla went before the Buddha, prostrated himself in greeting, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"My elder brother has invited the Buddha, and he wishes to invite all those who have newly arrived to a meal at his house; I pray that you will compassionately accept this invitation."

The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Ratnākara, the Bodhisattva Guhagupta, the Bodhisattva Naradatta, the Bodhisattva Susīma, the Bodhisattva Mahāsusārthavāha, the Bodhisattva Indradatta, and the Bodhisattva Varuṇadeva, together with their kinsmen, all came forward, touched their heads to the feet of the Buddha, and paid homage to the assembly of bhikṣus.

Having finished paying their respects, they departed from the Buddha’s presence and returned to the kingdom of Rājagṛha. Arriving at the house of the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, they assisted one another in preparing various provisions for the meal.
The Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām-Indra, and Brahmā Sahāmpati all came together in haste to assist the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla in preparing various provisions for the meal.

At that time, the kinsmen of the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla collectively adorned the city of Rājagṛha; they covered the entire kingdom with canopies of various kinds of fine silks, and hung silk banners in every street, lane, and marketplace. Throughout the whole land, flowers were scattered and incense was burned. For the sake of the Buddha, as well as for the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and all the poor and beggars, the provisions for the meal were prepared in equal measure for all.
Why is this? Because there is no partiality in giving; it is equal toward all people, including even the crawling and wriggling creatures.

Bhadrapāla, together with eight bodhisattvas and his kinsmen, went before the Buddha at mealtime. Prostrating himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew slightly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The meal is fully prepared; we pray that the Buddha will deign to proceed.
At that time, the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus all donned their robes and took up their bowls, and together they went to where the assembly had gathered, with everyone following them.
When the Buddha entered the kingdom of Rājagṛha and arrived at the house of the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla,
the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla had this thought: "Now, by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha,

may my house become exceedingly vast and entirely made of lapis lazuli, so that both the interior and exterior are visible to one another— those outside the city see all within my house, and those within my house see all outside the city."

The Buddha immediately knew the thoughts in Bhadrapāla’s mind; he then manifested his majestic spiritual power to cause Bhadrapāla’s house to become exceedingly vast, so that all the people within the kingdom could see them from within the house.
The Buddha entered the house of the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla and sat down; the community of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās each sat separately in their respective groups within the house.

When the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla saw that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were seated, he personally made offerings to the Buddha and the bhikṣus, serving hundreds of varieties of food with his own hands.

The Buddha, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, had all finished their meal; he gave equally to all those who were poor, providing each with sufficient food, all of which was made adequate through the grace of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.

When the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla saw that all the Buddha’s disciples had finished their meal, he first went forward to offer water for rinsing the mouth; finally, taking a small stool, he sat before the Buddha to listen to the sutra.

For the sake of the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla and the fourfold assembly of disciples, he preached the sutra; there was none who did not rejoice, none who did not delight in hearing it, and none who did not wish to hear it.
The Buddha invited the community of bhikṣus and his disciples by means of this sūtra; having risen, he departed together with the community of bhikṣus.

After the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla had finished eating, he went out from the city of Rājagṛha with his kinsmen and arrived at the place where the Buddha was. He came forward, paid homage to the Buddha, and all withdrew to sit on one side.

Then the Bodhisattvas Rāṣṭrapāla, Gadgadasvara, Naradatta, Susīma, Mahāsusārthavāha, Indradatta, Varuṇadeva, and Bhadrapāla, seeing that the assembly was all seated comfortably, stepped forward and asked the Buddha:
"By means of how many practices does a bodhisattva attain the samādhi of seeing all present Buddhas standing before one?"
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla:

"A bodhisattva attains the samādhi of swiftly beholding all present Buddhas standing before one through five practices: studying, upholding, practicing with earnestness, and having a mind that does not waver."
What are these five?

First, they delight in profound sutras without end, reaching no limit; they are entirely liberated from all calamities and transformations, freed from all defilements, and having departed from darkness, they enter into light, so that all obscurations are completely extinguished.
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:
“This bodhisattva has attained the joy of the dharma that comes from nowhere and has attained this samādhi.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!”
No longer taking pleasure in the realm of rebirth is the second;
no longer taking pleasure in or delighting in other paths is the third;
no longer taking pleasure in sensual desires is the fourth.
To maintain one's own conduct without limit is the fifth.
"Furthermore, there are five things by which a bodhisattva quickly attains this samādhi. What are these five?

First, one should not regret the mind of giving; one should have no greed and no attachment, and from this, one should harbor no expectations. After having given to others, one should never feel resentment.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

A bodhisattva practices giving by upholding this sutra and preaching it to others; what they say is peaceful, certain, and free from doubt; they have no sense of attachment or stinginess; and they personally practice and establish themselves within the profound words of the Buddha.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla! A bodhisattva is free from envy;
whatever he does is without doubt; he puts an end to sleep and sloth, puts an end to the five desires, does not speak of his own virtues, and likewise does not speak of the faults of others.
If there are those who revile one, or those who inflict punishment, one should neither become angry, nor harbor resentment, nor feel weary.
Why is this? Because one has entered into the practice of emptiness.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
A bodhisattva should personally study this samādhi and also teach it to others, copying this sutra onto fine silk so that it may endure for a long time.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
That which a bodhisattva believes in is manifold and joyful: they revere their elders and spiritual friends.
If they receive any gift from those who have newly begun their training, they should reflect upon repaying that kindness and always maintain mindfulness and faith.
If one receives a small gift from another and yet thinks of repaying it with something great, how much more so when the gift is abundant?
A bodhisattva always delights in honoring the sutras and discards any thought of ingratitude; by constantly mindful of being grateful, such a person attains samādhi swiftly.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Always delighting in the Dharma through profound understanding, Not giving rise to craving for any habitual desires,
Wandering through the five realms of existence without attachment— A practitioner who acts in this way attains samādhi."
Delighting in giving without seeking recompense, Bestowing gifts without attachment or lingering thought,
Granting them without perceiving a recipient— They desire only to attain liberation through the Buddha’s profound wisdom.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he practices giving; his mind leaps with joy, free from regret.
He constantly establishes himself in generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, as well as in the matters of diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom.

Fully endowed with the six perfections, they embrace all beings; With the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, And through skillful means and expedient wisdom, they rescue sentient beings; A practitioner who acts in this way attains samādhi.
If one gives rise to generosity and eliminates stinginess and greed, With a heart leaping with joy, they bestow their gifts;
Having given, they remain constantly delighted— A practitioner who acts in this way attains samādhi.
Clearly understanding the sūtras and dharmas and discerning their phrases, hearing the profound and essential meanings taught by the Buddha,
and expounding the subtle and wondrous transformation of the Way and its Virtue— the practitioner who acts thus attains samādhi.
If a person studies and recites this samādhi, fully understanding its wisdom and explaining it for others,
so that this Dharma of the sutra may endure forever— such a practitioner shall attain this samādhi.
Never concealing the profound and secret teachings of the Buddha’s sutras, he expounds them without seeking offerings;
seeking only the ground of peace and security in the Buddha-way, such a practitioner attains samādhi.
Removing attachments and casting off all hindrances, abandoning arrogance and great pride,
not praising oneself nor speaking of others' faults, one shall never again give rise to the notion of a self.
When one possesses a mind of tranquil concentration that does not arise, one is then able to understand this path of concentration and wisdom;
casting aside flattery and deceit, the mind becomes pure, and by means of this, one swiftly attains the patience of non-arising.
Always acting with utmost sincerity and free from artifice, their vows are fulfilled without deficiency;
planting many roots of right virtue and free from deviant conduct, those who love and delight in the Dharma attain the Way swiftly.

One who recites and studies the sūtras without ever forgetting them, and who constantly guards the prohibitions and precepts with pure conduct—such a practitioner shall swiftly attain Buddhahood; how much more so for one who reveres this samādhi of tranquility?
The Buddha told Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla:

"In the past, incalculable kalpas ago, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I heard this samādhi from Dīpaṃkara Buddha; I immediately received and upheld this samādhi, and beheld innumerable Buddhas of the ten directions, from all of whom I heard the sutras and received and upheld them."
At that time, all the Buddhas spoke to me, saying:
"After incalculable kalpas have passed, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
The Buddha then addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla:

"I tell you this for a reason: you yourselves shall now attain Buddhahood. You should all study this samādhi, for it is the foremost among internal dharmas that no other assembly can equal; it transcends all conceptualizations. Those who establish themselves within this samādhi will realize the path to Buddhahood."
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"I recall in the past, under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I attained this samādhi at that moment;
I immediately beheld countless Buddhas of the ten directions And heard them preach the profound and wondrous meaning of the Honored Dharma."
Just as a virtuous person goes to gather jewels and obtains whatever they hope for according to their wishes, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva:
seeking the jewel within the sutras, they immediately attain Buddhahood.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha:
"How, O God among Gods, should one maintain this samādhi?"
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla:
"One should not be attached to form, nor should one have a destination for rebirth; one should practice emptiness, and this samādhi should be maintained."
What is samādhi? One should practice in accordance with this Dharma. Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
The Bodhisattva observes his own body as being without a body; there is nothing observed, nothing seen, and nothing clung to.

Fundamentally, there is neither blindness nor deafness. As taught in the Dharma of the sutras, when vision abides, there is neither seeing nor clinging; to be without clinging is to be a guardian of the Way.
Within the Dharma there is nothing to doubt; one who does not doubt has seen the Buddha, and seeing the Buddha is the severing of doubt.
All dharmas do not come from anywhere to arise.
Why is this? If a bodhisattva has conceptualizations involving doubt regarding dharmas, they are thereby attached.
What constitutes attachment?

To hold that there is a person, there is a life-span, there is merit, there are aggregates, there is a person, there is resistance, there is perception, there are faculties, and there is desire—this is attachment.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva perceives all phenomena as being without attachment; he neither thinks of these phenomena nor perceives them.
What is meant by "not perceiving"?
For example, it is like a foolish person who studies other paths and is self-opinionated; such a person might say that there is a self, but a bodhisattva does not form such a view.
What, then, is the view of a bodhisattva?
For example, as seen by a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, an Avinivartanīya, a Pratyekabuddha, or an Arhat, there is neither joy nor sorrow;
a Bodhisattva who sees in this way likewise experiences neither joy nor sorrow;
one who maintains this samādhi also experiences neither joy nor sorrow.
"Just as space is without form, without conceptualization, pure, and free from defilement, so too does the bodhisattva perceive all phenomena.
With eyes unimpeded, they see all phenomena; by means of this, they behold all Buddhas."
He saw all the Buddhas as if a bright moon-pearl were placed upon lapis lazuli; like the sun when it first rises;
like the moon on the fifteenth day at the center of the host of stars;
like a Cakravartin king accompanied by his ministers; and like Śakra, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, in the midst of the gods.
Like the Brahma King seated at the highest point in the midst of the assembly of Brahmās; like a torch burning atop a high mountain peak;
like a king of physicians carrying medicine who travels about to cure the illnesses of others; like a lion emerging and walking alone;
like a flock of wild geese flying through the void with a leader in front; like [the moon] upon a high mountain in the winter month.
Snow accumulated on all four sides was visible; it was like the Great Boundary of Heaven and Earth,
like the Vajra Mountains repelling foul odors, like the waters below supporting the earth, like the wind supporting the waters so that all impurities are completely purified, like space itself,
and like the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven atop Mount Sumeru serving as its adornment.
The Buddhas are thus: through the Buddha’s observance of the precepts, the Buddha’s majestic power, and the Buddha’s merits, innumerable lands are all rendered utterly bright.
This Bodhisattva sees the Buddhas of the ten directions in this way and hears and fully receives all the sutras.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“The Buddha is free from defilement and detached from worldly toil; In his multitude of merits, he is ultimately without attachment.
Possessing great supernormal powers and wondrous sounds, The Dharma drum guides through meanings, surpassing all other tones.”
Awakened among the gods of gods, liberated through various wisdoms, They offer diverse incenses and flowers as worship;
Honoring the śarīra with countless virtues, With banners, canopies, and blended fragrances, they seek samādhi.
Having heard the Dharma, one universally and wondrously fulfills all learning; Far removed from inversion, this is likened to nirvāṇa.
One should never harbor attachment to the dharma of emptiness, But should resolve to understand the wondrous, unimpeded wisdom.
Pure as the moon rising with its radiance, like Brahmā established in his own palace, one should always maintain a pure mind and contemplate the World-Honored One;
with a mind free from attachment, one realizes the emptiness of non-characteristics.
Just as the snow on high mountains in winter, Or like a king, the most honored among men,
Or a pure mani jewel surpassing all other gems— One should contemplate the Buddha’s marks and signs in this way.
Like a king of geese flying with a guide before him, The void is pure, free from defilement and disorder;
The Buddha of purple-gold hue is likewise so— Sons of the Buddha, mindful of this, make offerings to the Honored One.
Dispelling all obscurity and removing darkness and folly, one immediately and swiftly attains the pure samādhi;
casting off all conceptual seeking, one achieves a concentrated mind free from defilement.
Free from the dust of afflictions, they shed all defilement; having cast away anger, they are without folly.
Their eyes are pure and naturally luminous, as they contemplate the Buddha’s merit without hindrance.
Contemplating the pure precepts of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, The mind is without attachment and seeks no signs;
One perceives neither self nor possessions, Nor does one give rise to various forms and appearances.
Abandoning birth and death, free from manifold views; casting off arrogance, their wisdom is pure;
far removing pride and not being self-aggrandizing; hearing of the samādhi of tranquility, they leave behind false views.
Any bhikṣus who are sons of the Buddha, faithful bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
or upāsikās who have eliminated greed and desire, shall attain this Dharma by practicing mindfulness and diligence.
Chapter Eleven: On Non-Perception. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla:
"If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to study this samādhi and swiftly attain it, they should first sever thoughts of form and abandon all self-conceit."
Having already severed discursive thought and being free from self-conceit, one should now train in this samādhi and not engage in contention.
What constitutes contention?
It is the disparagement of emptiness.
Therefore, one should not engage in disputes, nor should one revile others; one should simply recite this samādhi.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"If there are bodhisattvas who study and recite this samādhi, they shall establish themselves in ten matters therein."
What are the ten? First, when others offer bowls, bedding, or clothing, one does not feel envy.
Second, one should love and respect all people, and be filial and obedient toward elders.
Third, one should be reciprocal and mindful of repaying kindness;
fourth, one should not speak falsely and remain far removed from what is contrary to the Dharma;
fifth, one should always practice begging for food and not accept invitations.
Sixth, one should practice walking meditation with diligence;
seventh, one must not lie down to sleep during the day or night;
eighth, one should always desire to practice giving, cherishing nothing in the heavens or on earth, and never regretting it.
Ninth, to enter deeply into wisdom without attachment;
tenth, to first honor and serve a virtuous teacher as if they were a Buddha,
and only then recite this samādhi— these are the ten matters.
"When one practices in this manner according to the Dharma, one attains eight matters. What are these eight?
First, one attains ultimate purity in the precepts."
Second, not engaging in the affairs of other paths, but entering and emerging within wisdom;
third, being pure within wisdom and having no further craving for birth;
fourth, the eyes being pure and no longer desiring birth and death.
Fifth, being lofty and brilliant without attachment;
sixth, attaining Buddhahood through pure diligence;
seventh, not feeling elated when someone makes offerings to them.
"Eighth, being established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one no longer wavers.
These are the eight matters.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The wise do not give rise to conceptualizations; they cast aside arrogance and self-importance.
Always practicing patience without harshness or outflows—it is only thus that one studies this samādhi."
The wise person’s mind is luminous and does not contend with emptiness; signless, tranquil concentration is nirvāṇa.
Do not revile the Dharma, and do not dispute with the Buddha; one who practices in this way attains samādhi.
The wise one is thus free from pride, constantly mindful of the Buddha’s grace and the Dharma Master;
firmly abiding in pure faith with an unshakable resolve, they then train in this samādhi.
With a mind free from envy, one stays far from the darkness; Without giving rise to doubt, one always maintains faith.
One should practice diligence without indolence; A practitioner who acts in this way attains samādhi.

A bhikṣu who trains in this way always begs for alms; he does not go to invitations or assemblies, his mind is free from attachment, and he makes no hoardings. One who practices in this manner attains samādhi.
If one should obtain this Dharma teaching with one's own hands, and uphold and practice this sutra scroll,
having already fulfilled the intention to become like a Buddha, only then should one study and recite this samādhi.
Abiding in these supreme virtues and sincere faith, if there are those who study and recite this samādhi,
they will swiftly attain these eight dharmas— the pure and stainless teachings of all Buddhas.
That pure precept has its ultimate consummation; through flawless samādhi, one attains equal vision.
Regarding birth and death as empty and pure, one dwells in this Dharma and attains fulfillment.
Wisdom is pure and complete without remainder; one who acts without defilement is likewise unattached.
Having heard much, one gathers wisdom and discards what is vain; to practice in such a way is to be truly wise.
Those whose will is diligent lose nothing; being unattached to the benefits of offerings, they swiftly attain the unsurpassed path to Buddhahood. One who trains in such virtues is called wise.
Chapter Twelve: The Eighteen Unique Qualities and the Ten Powers. The Buddha said:
"One who attains these aforementioned eight matters shall obtain the eighteen matters of a Buddha."
What are the eighteen matters?

First, on a certain day he attained Buddhahood and on a certain day he entered parinirvāṇa; from the day he first attained Buddhahood until the day of his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha was free from all difficulties.
Second, he was without deficiency.
Third, there is no forgetfulness;
fourth, there is no lack of meditative concentration;
fifth, one never gives rise to the notion of phenomena or speaks of them as "mine."
Sixth, there is no time when one is unable to practice patience;
seventh, there is no time when one does not find joy;
eighth, there is no time when one does not apply diligence.
Ninth, there is no time when he is not mindful;
tenth, there is no time when he is not in samādhi;
eleventh, there is no time when he does not know.
Twelfth, there is no time when his wisdom of vision is not liberated;
thirteenth, regarding the events of incalculable past eons, there is nothing that can obstruct the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom of vision;
fourteenth, regarding the events of incalculable future eons, there is nothing that can obstruct the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom of vision.
Fifteenth, regarding the events of the countless worlds of the ten directions in the present, there is no one who can obstruct the Buddha’s unhindered wisdom when it perceives them;
sixteenth, the actions performed by his body have wisdom as their foundation and are always accompanied by wisdom;
seventeenth, the words spoken by his mouth have wisdom as their foundation and are always accompanied by wisdom.
"Eighteenth: Whatever matters the mind contemplates, wisdom is their foundation and they are always accompanied by wisdom;
these are the eighteen attributes of a Buddha.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"If there is a bodhisattva who, being free from further attachment, seeks the Dharma and fully protects it, one who studies this samādhi possesses ten protective dharmas.
What are these ten protective dharmas?"
The ten powers of a Buddha. What are these ten powers?
The first is the complete knowledge of that which is finite and that which is infinite.
Second, they fully know the origins and ends of the past, the future, and the present;
third, they fully know the liberation from and purification of meditative concentrations;
fourth, they fully know the various faculties, diligence, and the diverse objects of thought of all beings.
Fifth, he fully knows all that is believed;
sixth, he fully knows various transformations and immeasurable matters;
seventh, he understands them all, comprehends them all, and knows them all.
Eighth, they know all that is seen by the eye without any obstruction;
ninth, they know the infinite extent of both the beginning and the end;
tenth, they regard the past, future, and present as entirely equal, remaining free from any attachment or bias.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"If there is a bodhisattva who fully protects all dharmas that arise from nowhere, this bodhisattva shall attain the ten powers of a Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“The eighteen unique qualities of perfect enlightenment, and the ten powers currently manifest in the World-Honored One—
if one practices this samādhi, one will swiftly attain them before long.”
Chapter Thirteen: Encouragement and Assistance. The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:

“This bodhisattva possesses four matters by which he encourages and assists others in their joy within this samādhi. During the time of past Buddhas, he maintained this samādhi and assisted them in their joy;
those who study this sūtra shall themselves attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and their wisdom will be fully perfected—I likewise encourage and assist them in such joy.”
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

All future Buddhas who seek the bodhisattva path shall rejoice in this samādhi; those who study this samādhi shall themselves attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, fully perfecting their wisdom. In this way, they all assist in rejoicing.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

The countless Buddhas currently existing in the ten directions, when they were originally seeking the bodhisattva path, rejoiced in this samādhi; those who study this samādhi shall personally attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, their wisdom being fully perfected, and all [the Buddhas] rejoice in their merit.

May they, together with the people of the ten directions and all classes of crawling and flying creatures, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; by upholding this samādhi, may their merit of sympathetic joy assist them so that they may quickly attain this samādhi and before long realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"Regarding the merit of this bodhisattva within this samādhi, there are four matters that assist in generating joy; I shall provide a few similes for them."

Suppose there were a person with a lifespan of one hundred years who, from the moment they fell to the ground, walked for a full hundred years without ceasing; that person would travel faster than a swift wind, circling through the four directions, above, and below.
"What do you think, Bhadrapāla?
Is it possible for anyone to calculate the distance of that road? Bhadrapāla replied:
“No one is able to calculate its distance,
O God among Gods!
Only the Buddha’s disciple Śāriputra and the avaivartika bodhisattvas are able to calculate it.”
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla: “I therefore say to all bodhisattvas:

if there were good sons or good daughters who were to take all the lands of the four directions, above, and below—the places where such persons travel—and fill them with precious jewels to offer as alms to the Buddhas, it would not equal hearing this samādhi.”

If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing of this samādhi, rejoices in these four matters, their merit will surpass that of one who makes offerings to the Buddha by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, or even a hundred-millionfold.
"Do you see it, Bhadrapāla?
If a bodhisattva rejoices in this, would their merit not be great?"
For this reason, you should know that the merit of a bodhisattva who rejoices in these [virtues] is exceedingly sublime and great.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“In this teaching of the sutra, there are four matters for rejoicing;”
The World-Honored Ones of the past, the future, and the present,
Exhort and assist in the practice of meritorious deeds, To deliver all beings throughout the ten directions,
Even the smallest insects that crawl and fly, So that they may all attain equal enlightenment.
Suppose this entire circumference— throughout the four directions, above, and below—
were filled with people who live for a hundred years, walking without ceasing for the duration of their lives.
If one were to calculate the distance they have traveled, its measure would be difficult to fathom.
Only the disciples of the Buddha, the non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, know this:
to give offerings of precious jewels filling the entire world is not equal to hearing this Dharma;
the merit of the fourfold encouragement and assistance surpasses that [of such giving].
"Bhadra! Behold this:
the joy derived from these four matters is a hundred million times greater than that of giving;
it cannot be equaled by the merit of exhorting others to conversion. Chapter 14: The Buddha Siṃhamati At that time, the Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:

"In the distant past, during an incalculable, uncountable, immeasurable, and infinite *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa, there was a Buddha named Śikhin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—one whose majestic spiritual power was peerless, who brought peace to the world, who was the most honored among all scriptures, and who was proclaimed 'God among Gods' throughout the heavens above and the earth below—residing in a secluded place within that land."
This land of Jambudvīpa is abundant and fertile, and its people are numerous and happy.
At that time, the internal extent of Jambudvīpa was one hundred and eighty thousand koṭis of nayutas of yojanas.
At that time, within Jambudvīpa there were six million four hundred thousand kingdoms.
At that time, in Jambudvīpa there was a great kingdom named Badhanga, and in that country there were sixty billion people.
In this land dwelt the Buddha Śikhin.
There was a Cakravartin king named Vipaśyin who went to the place where the Buddha Śikhin was, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhāsa immediately knew what was in the king’s mind and thereupon preached this samādhi for him.
Upon hearing of this samādhi, the king rejoiced greatly; he took precious jewels and scattered them over the Buddha, thinking to himself:
"By means of this merit, may all the people of the ten directions attain peace and security."
"After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Sihakamati, King Vessikaṇṭha, at the end of his life, was reborn into a royal family as a crown prince named Brahmadatta."
At that time, in Jambudvīpa, there was a bhikṣu of high renown named Ratna. He then preached this samādhi to the fourfold assembly of disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

When Prince Brahmadata heard of this samādhi, he rejoiced with great joy; his heart leaped with delight as he heard this sūtra. He took precious jewels worth ten billion and scattered them over the bhikṣu, and further offered him fine robes, thereby resolving his mind to seek the Buddha-way.

At that time, together with a thousand people, he went to where that bhikṣu was; having shaved his head and beard to become a śramaṇa under that bhikṣu, he immediately sought instruction from him in this samādhi.
Together with a thousand bhikṣus, they served their teacher for eight thousand years without weariness or indolence; only once, at the beginning and end of this period, did they hear this samādhi.
Having heard this samādhi, these bhikṣus rejoiced through four matters of assistance and entered into lofty, sublime wisdom.

By virtue of this merit of rejoicing in assistance, he subsequently beheld sixty-eight thousand Buddhas; at each and every Buddha’s place, he heard this samādhi, personally maintained it, studied it, and further taught others to study it.
That person, by virtue of the merit of upholding this [teaching] and rejoicing in it, will later attain Buddhahood, named Tīrāviśeṣa-tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

At that time, these one thousand bhikṣus shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and become *tathāgatas*, *arhats*, and *samyak-saṃbuddhas*, all named Ti-lo-shou-lo-ü-ch'en; they shall teach incalculable numbers of people so that they all seek the Buddha-way.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"Who, upon hearing of this samādhi, would not rejoice in support?
Who would not study it?"
"Who is it that does not speak for others?
Who is it that does not maintain [the precepts]?
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
“If there is a bodhisattva who maintains this samādhi, they will swiftly attain Buddhahood. Bhadrapāla!
If there is a bodhisattva who hears from forty *li* away that there is one who maintains this samādhi, upon hearing it, that bodhisattva should immediately set out to seek him and go to his place.”
If one merely hears and knows that this samādhi exists, one should constantly seek it; how much more so if one actually hears and studies it?

Whether it be a hundred li away or as far as four thousand li, upon hearing that there is one who maintains this samādhi, one should go and study it until reaching that place. If merely hearing and knowing it is thus, how much more so if one actually hears and studies it?
The Buddha said:

"If one who lives far away should always go personally to seek it, how much more so for those who live ten or twenty *li* away—would they not go to seek and study it upon hearing that someone possesses this samādhi?"

Bhadra! If there is a bodhisattva who hears of this samādhi and desires to travel to where it is heard and sought, they should serve their teacher for ten years or a hundred years, providing them with complete offerings and attentive care.
This bodhisattva must not act according to his own will, but should follow the instructions of his teacher and always be mindful of the teacher’s kindness.
The Buddha said:

“I have therefore explained this for your sake: if a bodhisattva hears that there is a place four thousand *li* away where this samādhi is being taught, and he desires to go to that place, yet does not get to hear this samādhi;”
The Buddha said: "I tell you all:
because that person seeks through diligent practice, they shall never again lose the path to Buddhahood, but will surely attain Buddhahood for themselves."
Do you see it,
Bhadrapāla? When a bodhisattva hears this samādhi and resolves to seek it without ever being parted from it, the benefit they obtain is most sublime.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"I recall that in the past there was a Tathāgata, A Honored One among men named Śikhin.
At that time, there was a king who served as a master of the realm; He went before that Buddha and heard this samādhi."
With sincere intent and wise discernment, listen to this sutra; with immeasurable joy in heart, uphold the Dharma.
Then scatter precious jewels upon him, making offerings to Siṃhamati, the Honored One among Men.
With such thoughts in mind, he uttered this exclamation:
"In this very body, throughout future lives, I shall reverently practice the Buddha's teachings without daring to neglect them, and I shall likewise attain this samādhi."
By virtue of this merit and vow, at the end of his life, he shall immediately return to be born into a royal family;
there, he will behold a venerable great bhikṣu named Precious Wisdom, who is profoundly realized.
Hearing this samādhi at the proper time, they leaped for joy and immediately took it up;
they made offerings of billions of excellent things—precious jewels and exquisite garments—for the sake of the Way.
He immediately shaved his hair and beard along with a thousand others, coming with the aspiration and joy to seek this samādhi;
for eight thousand years they simultaneously fulfilled their practice, constantly following the bhikṣu without ever leaving him.
Once having heard it, one never hears it again; this samādhi is like the ocean.
One who upholds the sūtra scrolls, recites them, and explains them will hear this samādhi wherever they are born.
By virtue of accumulating these merits, one shall behold the great supernormal powers of the Buddhas;
for eighty thousand years, one shall fully possess them and immediately make offerings to every Buddha encountered.
I encountered sixty trillion Buddhas in the past, And further made offerings to six thousand honored ones;
Hearing the Dharma they preached, I was filled with great joy, And thereafter I beheld the Buddha Siṃha.
By virtue of this merit, may I be born into a royal family and behold a Buddha named Firm Diligence (*Dṛḍhavīrya*),
who transforms countless billions of people and delivers all beings from the afflictions of birth and death.
After studying and reciting this Dharma, one shall again behold a Buddha named Firm Valor (Dṛḍhavīrya);
his name is chanted throughout the heavens and the world, and by hearing the sound of this samādhi, one attains Buddhahood.
How much more so for those who receive, uphold, recite, and explain it?
Being unattached to any world-systems, they widely proclaim and disseminate this samādhi, never doubting or forgetting the Buddha-way.

This Samādhi Sūtra is the true word of the Buddha; if one hears that this sūtra exists in a distant land, one should go there to hear and receive it for the sake of the Way and the Dharma, reciting it with a single mind without forgetting or abandoning it.
Even if one were to go seeking it and fail to hear it, its merit and blessings would be inexhaustible;
no one could measure its virtuous meaning—how much more so for one who, having heard it, immediately receives and upholds it?
If there is one who desires this samādhi, They should reflect upon that Brahmāda of the past;
Instructing, practicing, and following his example without retreating— A bhikṣu who has attained this sūtra should act thus.
Chapter Fifteen: The Buddha of Sincerity. The Buddha said:
"In times long past, there was another Buddha named Satyanāma Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Varuṇa who, after that Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, maintained this samādhi.

At that time, I was a king of the Kṣatriya caste; I heard of this samādhi in a dream, and upon waking, I immediately went in search of the bhikṣu who maintained it, and followed him forthwith to become a śramaṇa so as to obtain it.
In this regard, a bhikṣu who hears this samādhi even once must serve his teacher for thirty-six thousand years; yet if demonic obstacles repeatedly arise, he may not hear it even once.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās:
“I speak thus to you all: you should swiftly take up this samādhi and never allow it to be forgotten or lost.”

One should serve one's teacher well and maintain this samādhi for one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas, without ever becoming weary or indolent; one must resolutely attain this samādhi.

One should not depart from the virtuous teacher; one should offer food, drink, requisites, clothing, bedding, and even tens of millions of precious jewels to the superior teacher, making offerings to the teacher without any sense of stinginess.
Should such things be lacking, one should go begging for food to provide for the teacher; one must strive to attain this samādhi without weariness.
The Buddha said:

"Setting aside these offerings, they are not even worth mentioning; one should always cut from one's own flesh to make offerings to a virtuous teacher, never begrudging one’s own body, let alone anything else."
One should serve a virtuous teacher as a servant serves his master; those who seek this samādhi should act in this way.
Having attained this samādhi, one should maintain it firmly and always be mindful of the teacher's kindness.
The Buddha said:

"This samādhi is difficult to encounter. Even if one were to seek this samādhi for a hundred billion kalpas, one might not even be able to hear its name, let alone learn it or further practice and teach it to others."
Even if one were to fill as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges with precious jewels and offer them in charity, would that merit not be great?
It would not equal the merit of one who writes down this samādhi and maintains its scroll; the latter’s merit is utterly incalculable.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"I recall my own past lives, When their duration was a full sixty thousand years;
I constantly followed the Dharma Master without ever leaving him, Yet at first, I did not hear this samādhi."
There was a Buddha named Its Utmost Sincerity; at that time, there was a bhikṣu named Haruṇa.
After that World-Honored Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣu constantly upheld this samādhi.
At that time, I was of the royal kṣatriya caste; in a dream, I heard of this samādhi.
The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita possesses this sūtra; Your Majesty should receive this meditative concentration from him.
Having awakened from the dream, he immediately went to seek him out;
he then beheld a bhikṣu upholding samādhi, whereupon he shaved his hair and beard to become a śramaṇa. For eight thousand years he studied, hearing [the teachings] all at once.
For a full span of eighty thousand years, he made offerings and served this bhikṣu;
yet during that time, although the conditions for Māra arose repeatedly, he never once heard [the Dharma] even a single time.
Therefore, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, as well as upāsakas and upāsikās, I entrust this sūtra-dharma to you; having heard this samādhi, quickly receive and practice it.
One should always respectfully study and uphold this Dharma-master, remaining diligent for the full duration of an eon without weariness;
one should not find even a thousand million difficulties too great for the sake of the Way, so that one may attain this Dharma-samādhi.
With robes, bedding, and couches numbering in the billions, the bhikṣu goes from house to house begging for alms to provide offerings to the Dharma Master; through such diligence, he attains samādhi.
Regarding lamps, food, and drink that ought to be obtained, as well as gold, silver, and precious jewels for offerings—
one should even cut off one's own flesh to provide such offerings, let alone mere food and drink.
The wise one who swiftly attains the Dharma and maintains its practice, who studies the sūtras with repeated recitation—this samādhi is difficult to encounter;
for billions of nayutas of kalpas, one should constantly seek it.
Wherever one wanders and hears this Dharma, one should proclaim it universally to all learners;
even if one were to seek it for billions of nayutas of kalpas, this samādhi would be difficult to hear.
Even if worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were filled with precious jewels used for giving,
if someone were to receive and respectfully recite even a single verse of this teaching, their merit would exceed that of the former.
Chapter Sixteen: The Seal of the Buddha The Buddha then spoke to Bhadrapāla:

"If there is a bodhisattva who hears this samādhi, upon hearing it, they should rejoice; they should study it; those who have studied it should, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, be enabled to study it; they should carefully transcribe this samādhi onto silk; they should receive the seal of the Buddha as their seal; and they should provide excellent offerings."
What is the Seal of the Buddha?

It is that what is known should not be practiced; there is no greed, no seeking, no conceptualization, no attachment, no aspiration, no destination for rebirth, no going forth, no arising, no possession, no grasping, no looking back, no departing, no obstruction, no existence, no fetter; all that exists is exhausted, all that is desired is exhausted; there is no source from which it arises, no cessation, no destruction, and no decay.
The essential path and the root of the path reside within the seal; it cannot be destroyed, cannot be defeated, and cannot be impaired by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
The ignorant may doubt this seal, yet this seal is the Seal of the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Now, as I speak this samādhi, one thousand eight hundred billion devas, asuras, ghosts and spirits, nāgas, and human beings have all attained the stage of srotāpanna;
eight hundred bhikṣus have all attained the stage of arhat."
Five hundred bhikṣuṇīs all attained the path of arhatship;
ten thousand bodhisattvas all attained this samādhi, all attained the joy of the dharma of non-arising, and stood therein;
and twelve thousand bodhisattvas were no longer subject to regression.

The Buddha spoke to Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the bhikṣu Ānanda, the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the bodhisattva Ratnākara, the bodhisattva Guhagupta, the bodhisattva Naradatta, the bodhisattva Susīma, the bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the bodhisattva Indradatta, and the bodhisattva Varuṇadeva.
The Buddha said:

"Since I first sought the path to Buddhahood incalculable eons ago, I have now attained it as a Buddha. I entrust this sutra to you all; study, recite, uphold, and preserve it without ever forgetting or losing it."
"Bhadrapāla, if there are bodhisattvas who study this samādhi, they should study it with complete stability and attentiveness.
Those who wish to hear it should hear it completely; those who explain it to others should explain it completely."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla and his companions, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the bhikṣu Ānanda, and all the devas, asuras, nāgas, spirits, and humans were greatly rejoiced. They prostrated themselves before the Buddha and departed.
